SBURB RECREATION PROJECT SESSION GENERATION SPECIFICATION Version 1.0 —
6 November 2026

PURPOSE This document specifies the first major subsystem of a
browser-based recreation of human SBURB, inspired by the mechanics and
events depicted in Homestuck. It is intended as a handoff document for
an AI game-generation tool.

The immediate goal is NOT to implement all of SBURB. The immediate goal
is to generate a coherent, inspectable session: its players, Classpects,
server/client network, entry order, Lands, Consorts, quests, Denizens,
and initial session conditions.

The game should support both fully randomized generation and guided
generation in which the creator supplies constraints or fixed choices.

PROJECT DECISIONS — FIXED - Game scope: human SBURB only. Do not
implement SGRUB-specific mechanics in this version. - Classpects: use
the twelve established Classes and twelve established Aspects as the
foundation. Keep the content model extensible for custom Classes,
Aspects, and interpretations. - Generation: provide both Randomized
Session and Guided Session modes, selectable at session creation. -
Multiplayer: simulate multiple players locally; actual online
multiplayer is not required. - Platform: browser-based HTML, CSS, and
JavaScript. - Development approach: modular and incremental. Preserve
working features when extending the game. - Reproducibility: save a
session seed and all generated session data so that a session can be
reopened and inspected. If practical, allow regeneration from the same
seed and configuration.

IMPORTANT CANON POLICY Homestuck does not provide a complete technical
manual for every game mechanic. Keep three categories distinct
throughout the project:

1.  CANON ANCHOR: A fact or concept directly established by the comic.
2.  INTERPRETATION: A reasonable reading of material that is
    demonstrated but not exhaustively defined.
3.  IMPLEMENTATION RULE: A practical rule invented for this playable
    recreation.

Do not label fan interpretations or invented mechanics as official
canon. Where a rule is uncertain, mark it as configurable or provisional
rather than presenting it as settled fact.

CORE DESIGN PRINCIPLES - Generate a session, not merely a set of
unrelated character sheets. - Generated systems must share data.
Prototyping should influence session state; player connections should
affect entry logistics; Land quests should connect to their Consorts and
Denizens. - Guided inputs are constraints. The generator must not
silently replace a creator’s explicit choices. - Randomness should be
seeded and reproducible. - Generated content should be coherent and
explainable. Each generated Land, quest, and complication should have a
short explanation of how its pieces relate. - Avoid arbitrary numerical
character statistics in this phase. Classpects are thematic identities,
not automatically combat classes with canonically defined damage
values. - Provide an editable session summary before starting
gameplay. - Use readable names, descriptions, and clear controls. The
first version should prioritize a functional generator over elaborate
graphics.

1.  SESSION CREATION SCREEN

Provide a New Session flow with the following settings.

REQUIRED SETTINGS - Session name: user-provided or automatically
generated. - Generation mode: Randomized Session or Guided Session. -
Player count: configurable. Use a sensible default such as four players,
but do not hard-code four as the only valid size. - Random seed:
automatically generated by default; optionally editable or displayed. -
Difficulty: optional implementation setting. Suggested choices: Relaxed,
Standard, Challenging, and Severe. These are game-implementation labels,
not Homestuck canon categories.

OPTIONAL SETTINGS - Number of players. - Fixed or randomized
Classpects. - Fixed or randomized server/client relationships. - Fixed
or randomized Prospit/Derse affiliations. - Land themes or environmental
preferences. - Desired tone (for example: adventurous, mysterious,
eerie, whimsical, or dangerous). - Session complications: disabled,
standard, or elevated. - Custom content enabled/disabled.

The creator should be able to leave any optional setting unset. Unset
values are generated automatically.

2.  PLAYER GENERATION

Each player record should contain at least:

-   Unique player ID.
-   Display name.
-   Optional pronouns or character description, if supplied by the
    creator.
-   Class.
-   Aspect.
-   Full Title, formatted as “Class of Aspect”.
-   Dream moon: Prospit or Derse.
-   Kernelsprite record.
-   Server player ID, if any.
-   Client player ID(s), if any.
-   Entry order.
-   Land record ID.
-   Generation notes explaining which values were fixed and which were
    randomized.

Do not invent personal details such as a player’s personality,
appearance, or biography unless the creator asks for character
generation. The generator may offer optional personality prompts, but
should not overwrite supplied character information.

2A. CLASSES

The twelve established Classes are: - Heir - Seer - Knight - Page -
Mage - Rogue - Thief - Prince - Bard - Maid - Sylph - Witch

Store Class definitions as data rather than embedding them in generation
logic. Each definition should support: - Canon name. - Short
description. - Longer interpretive description. - Source/status note. -
Optional implementation notes. - Custom/official flag.

Class interpretations vary, and the comic does not provide a complete
ability specification for every Class. Do not generate definitive canon
ability trees. For this stage, a Class supplies a thematic description
and may later inform ability design.

2B. ASPECTS

The twelve established Aspects are: - Time - Space - Light - Void -
Heart - Mind - Rage - Hope - Life - Doom - Breath - Blood

Store Aspect definitions as data. Each should support: - Canon name. -
Core thematic keywords. - Short description. - Longer interpretive
description. - Source/status note. - Optional implementation notes. -
Custom/official flag.

The keywords and descriptions should be treated as thematic guides, not
exhaustive mechanical definitions.

2C. CLASSPECT ASSIGNMENT

A standard Classpect consists of one Class and one Aspect. The
twelve-by-twelve foundation provides 144 possible combinations.

Randomized mode: - Select one valid Class and one valid Aspect for each
player. - Avoid duplicate Classpects by default when enough combinations
are available, but do not prohibit duplicates unless the creator enables
a uniqueness setting. - Do not imply that random assignment is a
canonical method of determining a Title.

Guided mode: - Allow the creator to lock a player’s Class, Aspect, or
complete Classpect independently. - Randomize only the unassigned
components. - Preserve all locked values exactly. - Allow custom Classes
or Aspects only when custom content is enabled.

Do not automatically infer a player’s personality, morality, destiny, or
behavior from their Classpect.

3.  SERVER/CLIENT NETWORK

SBURB uses server/client relationships. In this recreation, simulate
these relationships as a directed network.

TERMS - Server player: the player who operates the game interface and
deploys or manipulates game machinery for another player. - Client
player: the player whose game environment is being operated on by their
server. - Initial host: the player who begins the session’s game
installation/hosting process. This is a session role for the simulation
and should not be confused with every later server relationship.

A player may be a client to one player and a server to another. Do not
restrict the network to a simple star with one server and many clients.

NETWORK DATA For each player, store: - Their server player’s ID, if
assigned. - A list of their client players’ IDs. - Their entry order. -
Connection status.

VALIDATION - No player may be their own server. - Connections must
reference existing players. - Do not create contradictory or duplicate
connections. - The network must not contain an impossible dependency
cycle for entry. A player cannot be required to enter before the player
whose server assistance is necessary for that entry. - Show the network
visually and provide a readable text explanation.

GENERATION Randomized mode: - Generate a valid connected or
intentionally partitioned network, depending on the session
configuration. - Choose an initial host. - Determine an entry order
compatible with the dependency relationships. - If a valid network
cannot be produced under the current constraints, explain the conflict
and offer to regenerate or relax constraints.

Guided mode: - Let the creator select each player’s server
relationship. - Validate the network before generation. - Explain any
invalid dependency or cycle and request correction rather than silently
changing the network.

Do not assume that every player must have exactly one client or that all
sessions must use the same network shape.

4.  ENTRY SEQUENCE

The entry sequence should be represented as a set of ordered events, not
just a single “enter game” button.

CANON ANCHORS The human SBURB entry process involves game machinery
including: - Cruxtruder: releases the Cruxite Dowel and initiates a
meteor countdown. - Totem Lathe: carves the dowel using a pattern
supplied through the entry process. - Alchemiter: produces the Cruxite
artifact from the carved dowel. - Kernelsprite: is created/prototyped as
part of the entry process. - Cruxite artifact: is used to complete
entry.

At a high level, the player and their home are transported into the
Medium when the entry artifact is activated/destroyed.

IMPLEMENTATION For each player, track: - Machinery deployed. -
Kernelsprite created. - First prototyping completed. - Entry artifact
pattern available. - Dowel carved. - Artifact created. - Entry
completed. - Meteor countdown state.

The entry screen should communicate which actions are complete and what
remains. For the initial generator, it is acceptable to generate an
entry plan and status summary rather than fully simulate the machinery
interactions.

ENTRY ORDER Entry order must respect the server/client dependency graph.
The game should not claim a client can complete a step requiring server
deployment before that server has entered or otherwise made the required
deployment possible.

5.  KERNELSPRITES AND PROTOTYPING

Each player receives a Kernelsprite. A Kernelsprite is a guide/companion
and is affected by prototyping.

CANON ANCHORS - Prototyping changes the Sprite. - Prototyping has
consequences beyond the Sprite itself, including effects on the
session’s enemies and the royal powers associated with the game. - The
timing of prototyping matters. Pre-entry and post-entry prototyping can
have different consequences. - The normal process is associated with two
prototyping opportunities, though unusual circumstances can alter
events.

PLAYER DATA Each Kernelsprite should record: - Sprite ID. - Owner player
ID. - Base appearance/description. - First prototyping input. - First
prototyping timing. - Second prototyping input. - Second prototyping
timing. - Resulting appearance/personality/abilities. - Session-wide
consequences.

GENERATION In guided mode, allow the creator to specify prototyping
inputs or leave them random. In randomized mode, generate plausible
inputs from a library of objects, creatures, characters, or other
entities.

Do not reduce prototyping to a cosmetic adjective or a simple numerical
buff. It should create persistent session tags/effects that other
systems can inspect.

For the first implementation, create a structured list of prototyping
tags and consequences. Keep their exact effects configurable and clearly
marked as implementation rules.

6.  DREAM MOONS

Each player is associated with a dream self on either Prospit or Derse.

CANON ANCHORS - Prospit and Derse are the two dream moons. - A player’s
dream self can act and experience events separately from their waking
self. - Dream selves and waking selves have distinct states and can be
affected separately.

PLAYER DATA - Dream moon. - Dream-self status. - Dream-self location. -
Dream-self health/status, if health is implemented. - Relevant dream
events.

For the session generator, assign Prospit or Derse either randomly or by
creator choice. Do not claim that a simple random assignment is the
canonical determination method.

7.  LAND GENERATION

Every player receives an individual Land in the Medium.

LAND NAME Use the familiar naming format: “Land of [Noun] and [Noun]”

The two defining nouns should be meaningful and evocative. They may
describe environmental features, recurring motifs, problems, or thematic
ideas. Do not simply concatenate two unrelated random words.

LAND RECORD Each Land should contain: - Unique Land ID. - Owner player
ID. - Land name. - Primary environment/biome. - Secondary environment or
contrasting feature. - Geography. - Major landmarks. - Settlements. -
Consort species and society. - Central problem. - Cause/history of the
problem. - Main quest. - Optional quest branches. - Denizen and
Denizen’s domain. - Seven Gates and their states. - Enemy/Underling
encounter themes. - Resource/grist notes. - Generation rationale
connecting the Land to the player’s Aspect and Classpect.

LAND GENERATION LOGIC Generate a coherent combination of: 1. Two Land
title nouns. 2. A physical environment. 3. A central problem. 4. A cause
for that problem. 5. A quest that addresses the problem. 6. A Denizen
and a final challenge. 7. Consorts who have a reason to care about the
problem.

Aspect should influence the Land’s motifs and quest, but should not
dictate every detail. Classpect may provide additional thematic
inspiration. Avoid a simplistic one-to-one mapping such as “all Time
players receive clock planets.”

In guided mode, allow the creator to lock one or both title nouns, a
biome, a motif, or a quest theme. Generate the remaining details around
those constraints.

8.  CONSORTS AND LAND POPULATIONS

Consorts are native inhabitants of the Lands. They are characters and
societies, not merely decorative monsters.

Generate for each Land: - A Consort species or visual archetype. - A
short description. - A settlement or society. - Cultural details or
customs. - A few named NPCs with distinct roles. - Their understanding
of the Land’s central problem. - Quest hooks or information they can
provide.

Consort species and societies should be varied. Do not assume all Lands
have the same species, culture, or political structure.

NPC records should include: - Name. - Role. - Brief personality or
conversational style. - Relevant knowledge. - Quest connection. -
Current status.

Do not generate excessive dialogue in the first version. A few useful
dialogue options and quest explanations are sufficient.

9.  DENIZENS

Each Land has a Denizen, an exceptionally powerful entity associated
with the Land’s ultimate challenge.

Known examples include Echidna, Typheus, Cetus, and Hephaestus.

DENIZEN RECORD - Name. - Land ID. - Mythological/creature archetype. -
Domain or lair. - Temperament. - Connection to the Land’s central
problem. - Challenge or trial. - Possible outcomes. - Relevant reward or
progression flag.

Do not assume every Denizen is simply a boss that must be killed. The
encounter may involve a choice, test, bargain, confrontation, or other
resolution.

The Denizen and its challenge should be related to the Land’s quest and
the player’s Aspect, without forcing every player into the same kind of
encounter.

10. SEVEN GATES AND LAND PROGRESSION

Each Land has seven Gates forming a progression route toward Skaia.

For the generator, create seven distinct Gate records: - Gate number (1
through 7). - Location or landmark. - Requirement to reach or unlock
it. - Challenge/obstacle. - Destination or progression effect. -
Locked/unlocked/completed status.

The server player’s assistance in constructing and deploying the
client’s house is part of the broader progression structure.

Do not invent a detailed universal gate-placement formula and label it
canon. Gate placement, obstacles, and unlock conditions may be
implementation-generated, provided they are consistent and clearly
identified as such.

11. SESSION-WIDE INITIAL CONDITIONS

The session generator should produce a global session record
containing: - Session ID and name. - Generation mode. - Seed. - Player
roster. - Server/client graph. - Entry order. - Number of players
entered. - Prototyping records. - Initial Battlefield state. - Prospit
and Derse state. - Initial meteor countdowns, where relevant. - Session
difficulty setting. - Complication level. - Generation warnings and
notes.

The Battlefield is affected by player entry and prototyping. The
generator should therefore use the roster, entry sequence, and
prototyping records when establishing the initial Battlefield state.

Do not treat the Battlefield as an unrelated decorative location. It is
part of the session’s shared state.

12. RANDOMIZED AND GUIDED GENERATION MODES

RANDOMIZED SESSION - The creator supplies only required settings, such
as player count and session name. - Generate all remaining values using
the session seed. - Produce a complete session overview. - Avoid
duplicate Classpects by default when possible, without treating
duplicates as invalid. - Generate a valid server/client network and
entry order. - Ensure each player receives a coherent Land, Consort
population, quest, and Denizen. - Generate prototyping inputs and
initial conditions. - Display a summary and allow the creator to inspect
each player’s details.

GUIDED SESSION - The creator can lock specific values and leave others
unspecified. - Support partial configuration: for example, a creator may
specify player names and Classpects while randomizing Lands and
connections. - Explicitly locked values must never be overwritten. -
Generated values should be designed around the locked values. - Validate
dependencies and explain conflicts. - Allow the creator to revise a
choice and regenerate only dependent content when practical.

BOTH MODES - Display which values were manually specified and which were
generated. - Show the seed. - Allow saving and loading. - Provide a
“regenerate” action with clear scope: regenerate the entire session or
only a selected section. - If a section is regenerated, preserve locked
values and avoid breaking references to other session data.

13. DATA MODEL AND CODE ORGANIZATION

Use modular JavaScript data structures. Keep definitions separate from
generation functions and UI rendering.

Suggested top-level data objects:

Session: - id - name - seed - mode - settings - players[] -
connections[] - entryOrder[] - lands[] - battlefield - globalEvents[] -
generationLog[]

Player: - id - name - classId - aspectId - title - dreamMoon -
serverId - clientIds[] - entryOrder - spriteId - landId - dreamSelf -
generationLog[]

Land: - id - ownerId - name - environment - geography - landmarks[] -
consorts - quest - denizen - gates[] - resources - enemies -
generationLog[]

Sprite: - id - ownerId - prototyping[] - tags[] - description -
effects[]

Use stable IDs rather than relying on array positions. Keep a central
registry or clearly organized data definitions for Classes, Aspects,
Consort archetypes, Land motifs, Denizens, and generation tables.

A seeded random-number generator is strongly preferred. Do not use
unrelated calls to Math.random() throughout the code if doing so makes a
session impossible to reproduce.

14. USER INTERFACE REQUIREMENTS

The first playable version should include:

A. Main menu - New Session. - Load Session, if saving is implemented. -
Help/Mechanics Reference.

B. Session setup - Randomized or Guided mode. - Player count. - Session
name. - Seed. - Optional configuration fields.

C. Player roster - Player cards. - Classpect display. - Dream moon. -
Server/client relationship. - Entry order.

D. Session network - A readable visual diagram of server/client
relationships. - Clear indication of the initial host. - Validation
warnings.

E. Land overview - One card per player. - Land name and environment. -
Consort species. - Central quest. - Denizen. - Gate progression.

F. Session summary - Global conditions. - Prototyping consequences. -
Battlefield state. - Warnings and unusual circumstances.

The interface should be navigable on a typical desktop browser and
remain usable on a mobile screen. Prioritize clarity and functional
controls over decorative complexity.

15. VALIDATION AND QUALITY CHECKS

Before accepting a generated session, validate:

-   Every player has a unique ID.
-   Every player has exactly one valid Class and one valid Aspect.
-   Every player has one Land.
-   Every Land has exactly seven Gate records.
-   Every Land has a Consort population.
-   Every Land has a Denizen record.
-   Every player has a Kernelsprite record.
-   Every connection references an existing player.
-   No player is their own server.
-   Entry dependencies are valid and do not form an impossible cycle.
-   Every Land and quest has enough information to be understandable.
-   Every generated reference uses a valid ID.
-   The seed and generation settings are saved.

If generation fails validation, do not silently display a broken
session. Explain the problem and offer regeneration or correction.

16. OUT OF SCOPE FOR THIS FIRST MILESTONE

Do not attempt to implement all of the following in the initial build: -
Full turn-based combat. - Complete enemy stat blocks. - Full Grist
economy. - Complete alchemy and every possible item combination. - Fully
interactive Sylladex/Fetch Modus system. - Complete Echeladder
progression. - Full seven-Gate exploration gameplay. - Complete
dream-world exploration. - God Tier ascension. - The Reckoning as a
playable real-time event. - Time travel and doomed timelines. - The
Scratch. - The Ultimate Alchemy as a complete endgame system. - Actual
online multiplayer.

These are future milestones. The first build should focus on producing a
coherent session generator with inspectable, interconnected data.

17. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA

The first build is successful if a user can:

1.  Open the game in a browser.
2.  Start a new human SBURB session.
3.  Select Randomized or Guided generation.
4.  Configure a roster of multiple players.
5.  Generate or specify each player’s Classpect.
6.  Generate or specify a valid server/client network.
7.  Obtain a valid entry order.
8.  Generate a unique Land for each player.
9.  Inspect each Land’s Consorts, quest, Denizen, and seven Gates.
10. Inspect each player’s Kernelsprite and prototyping information.
11. Review the initial session-wide conditions.
12. Save and reopen the generated session, or otherwise preserve its
    seed and data.
13. See clear explanations when constraints conflict or generation
    fails.

A session should feel like one interconnected game scenario, not a
random list of names and descriptions.

18. INSTRUCTIONS TO THE GAME GENERATOR

Build the first milestone as a functional browser-based application
using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

Prioritize a working session-generation flow and reliable data handling.
Use modular functions and structured data. Keep content definitions
separate from generation logic and UI rendering.

Do not attempt to implement every future SBURB feature now. Do not
replace the requested systems with a generic fantasy RPG. Do not invent
official canon rules where the comic is ambiguous. Label
implementation-specific assumptions.

Make all primary controls functional. Generated data must be internally
consistent and visible to the user. Include useful error messages and
validation. If a feature cannot be implemented, state that limitation
rather than presenting a nonfunctional button.

The deliverable should be a usable first version of the SBURB Session
Generator, not merely a static mockup or a description of a proposed
game.

END OF SPECIFICATION

## Objective
- Build a complete, playable browser-based human SBURB session generator from the attached specification.
- Deliver a coherent, seeded session with inspectable players, network, entry sequence, Lands, Consorts, Denizens, Gates, and session conditions.

## Requirements
- Support Randomized and Guided modes, configurable player count, editable seed, locked player choices, and preserve explicit constraints.
- Generate reproducible, interconnected session data; validate the network and generated records; support saving/loading and exporting.
- Keep canon anchors, interpretations, and implementation rules clearly distinguished.
- Provide usable desktop and mobile UI with functional controls; do not imply unimplemented features are functional.
- The user requested no clarifying questions and brief assumptions at completion.

## Decisions
- Implemented as a modular plain HTML/CSS/JavaScript app with data definitions separated from generation and rendering.
- Used a seeded RNG, acyclic server tree, generated Land/quest/Consort/Denizen/Gate data, and descriptive prototyping effects.
- Current UI uses an atmospheric dark console aesthetic and responsive layouts.

## Work State
### Completed
- Retrieved and read the specification from `https://omgithub.com/api/issue-attachments/ae9b3937-7d69-4d81-9983-e2ebd2f58f10`.
- Created `index.html` with welcome, setup, session, tab navigation, import dialog, and app script/style references.
- Created `style.css` with responsive styling for the planned screens and components.
- Began `app.js`: content registries, seeded generation, guided player constraints, generated session data, validation, and renderers for overview, players, network, Lands, entry sequence, and reference sections are present.

### Active
- Finish `app.js`; the file currently ends after `referenceHtml()` and lacks event binding, entry/gate action handlers, save/load/import/export, app initialization, and closing IIFE.
- Test the full setup-to-session flow, verify JavaScript parses, fix bugs, and capture/inspect a screenshot.
- Check `index.html` startup works with the repository’s runtime.

### Blocked
- The app is incomplete and is not yet runnable as a complete experience because `app.js` lacks initialization and event handlers.

## Next Move
1. Continue `app.js` with `bindTabEvents`, setup/menu/tab/button event listeners, network edits with cycle validation and order recalculation, entry progression, gate progression, save/load/export/import, toast/help behavior, and initial setup.
2. Review generated data and UI for consistency and edge cases, then run the app and browser checks.
3. Fix issues and report implemented scope and any remaining limitations.

## Relevant Files
- `index.html`: Main app screens and DOM hooks.
- `app.js`: Session generation and partial rendering implementation; primary continuation point.
- `style.css`: Responsive visual design and component styles.
- `/tmp/opencode/SBurb_Session_Generation_Specification.txt`: Retrieved complete build specification.

## Important Context
- `app.js` already defines `CLASSES`, `ASPECTS`, `SETTINGS`, seeded RNG helpers, `generate()`, `validateSession()`, `topologicalOrder()`, renderers, and `ENTRY_STEPS`.
- Session model includes `players`, `connections`, `entryOrder`, `lands`, `sprites`, `battlefield`, `globalEvents`, `warnings`, and per-player `entryState`.
- No tests or browser verification have been run; changes are uncommitted.

1: SBURB RECREATION PROJECT SESSION GENERATION SPECIFICATION Version 1.0 —
2: 6 November 2026
3: 
4: PURPOSE This document specifies the first major subsystem of a
5: browser-based recreation of human SBURB, inspired by the mechanics and
6: events depicted in Homestuck. It is intended as a handoff document for
7: an AI game-generation tool.
8: 
9: The immediate goal is NOT to implement all of SBURB. The immediate goal
10: is to generate a coherent, inspectable session: its players, Classpects,
11: server/client network, entry order, Lands, Consorts, quests, Denizens,
12: and initial session conditions.
13: 
14: The game should support both fully randomized generation and guided
15: generation in which the creator supplies constraints or fixed choices.
16: 
17: PROJECT DECISIONS — FIXED - Game scope: human SBURB only. Do not
18: implement SGRUB-specific mechanics in this version. - Classpects: use
19: the twelve established Classes and twelve established Aspects as the
20: foundation. Keep the content model extensible for custom Classes,
21: Aspects, and interpretations. - Generation: provide both Randomized
22: Session and Guided Session modes, selectable at session creation. -
23: Multiplayer: simulate multiple players locally; actual online
24: multiplayer is not required. - Platform: browser-based HTML, CSS, and
25: JavaScript. - Development approach: modular and incremental. Preserve
26: working features when extending the game. - Reproducibility: save a
27: session seed and all generated session data so that a session can be
28: reopened and inspected. If practical, allow regeneration from the same
29: seed and configuration.
30: 
31: IMPORTANT CANON POLICY Homestuck does not provide a complete technical
32: manual for every game mechanic. Keep three categories distinct
33: throughout the project:
34: 
35: 1.  CANON ANCHOR: A fact or concept directly established by the comic.
36: 2.  INTERPRETATION: A reasonable reading of material that is
37:     demonstrated but not exhaustively defined.
38: 3.  IMPLEMENTATION RULE: A practical rule invented for this playable
39:     recreation.
40: 
41: Do not label fan interpretations or invented mechanics as official
42: canon. Where a rule is uncertain, mark it as configurable or provisional
43: rather than presenting it as settled fact.
44: 
45: CORE DESIGN PRINCIPLES - Generate a session, not merely a set of
46: unrelated character sheets. - Generated systems must share data.
47: Prototyping should influence session state; player connections should
48: affect entry logistics; Land quests should connect to their Consorts and
49: Denizens. - Guided inputs are constraints. The generator must not
50: silently replace a creator’s explicit choices. - Randomness should be
51: seeded and reproducible. - Generated content should be coherent and
52: explainable. Each generated Land, quest, and complication should have a
53: short explanation of how its pieces relate. - Avoid arbitrary numerical
54: character statistics in this phase. Classpects are thematic identities,
55: not automatically combat classes with canonically defined damage
56: values. - Provide an editable session summary before starting
57: gameplay. - Use readable names, descriptions, and clear controls. The
58: first version should prioritize a functional generator over elaborate
59: graphics.
60: 
61: 1.  SESSION CREATION SCREEN
62: 
63: Provide a New Session flow with the following settings.
64: 
65: REQUIRED SETTINGS - Session name: user-provided or automatically
66: generated. - Generation mode: Randomized Session or Guided Session. -
67: Player count: configurable. Use a sensible default such as four players,
68: but do not hard-code four as the only valid size. - Random seed:
69: automatically generated by default; optionally editable or displayed. -
70: Difficulty: optional implementation setting. Suggested choices: Relaxed,
71: Standard, Challenging, and Severe. These are game-implementation labels,
72: not Homestuck canon categories.
73: 
74: OPTIONAL SETTINGS - Number of players. - Fixed or randomized
75: Classpects. - Fixed or randomized server/client relationships. - Fixed
76: or randomized Prospit/Derse affiliations. - Land themes or environmental
77: preferences. - Desired tone (for example: adventurous, mysterious,
78: eerie, whimsical, or dangerous). - Session complications: disabled,
79: standard, or elevated. - Custom content enabled/disabled.
80: 
81: The creator should be able to leave any optional setting unset. Unset
82: values are generated automatically.
83: 
84: 2.  PLAYER GENERATION
85: 
86: Each player record should contain at least:
87: 
88: -   Unique player ID.
89: -   Display name.
90: -   Optional pronouns or character description, if supplied by the
91:     creator.
92: -   Class.
93: -   Aspect.
94: -   Full Title, formatted as “Class of Aspect”.
95: -   Dream moon: Prospit or Derse.
96: -   Kernelsprite record.
97: -   Server player ID, if any.
98: -   Client player ID(s), if any.
99: -   Entry order.
100: -   Land record ID.
101: -   Generation notes explaining which values were fixed and which were
102:     randomized.
103: 
104: Do not invent personal details such as a player’s personality,
105: appearance, or biography unless the creator asks for character
106: generation. The generator may offer optional personality prompts, but
107: should not overwrite supplied character information.
108: 
109: 2A. CLASSES
110: 
111: The twelve established Classes are: - Heir - Seer - Knight - Page -
112: Mage - Rogue - Thief - Prince - Bard - Maid - Sylph - Witch
113: 
114: Store Class definitions as data rather than embedding them in generation
115: logic. Each definition should support: - Canon name. - Short
116: description. - Longer interpretive description. - Source/status note. -
117: Optional implementation notes. - Custom/official flag.
118: 
119: Class interpretations vary, and the comic does not provide a complete
120: ability specification for every Class. Do not generate definitive canon
121: ability trees. For this stage, a Class supplies a thematic description
122: and may later inform ability design.
123: 
124: 2B. ASPECTS
125: 
126: The twelve established Aspects are: - Time - Space - Light - Void -
127: Heart - Mind - Rage - Hope - Life - Doom - Breath - Blood
128: 
129: Store Aspect definitions as data. Each should support: - Canon name. -
130: Core thematic keywords. - Short description. - Longer interpretive
131: description. - Source/status note. - Optional implementation notes. -
132: Custom/official flag.
133: 
134: The keywords and descriptions should be treated as thematic guides, not
135: exhaustive mechanical definitions.
136: 
137: 2C. CLASSPECT ASSIGNMENT
138: 
139: A standard Classpect consists of one Class and one Aspect. The
140: twelve-by-twelve foundation provides 144 possible combinations.
141: 
142: Randomized mode: - Select one valid Class and one valid Aspect for each
143: player. - Avoid duplicate Classpects by default when enough combinations
144: are available, but do not prohibit duplicates unless the creator enables
145: a uniqueness setting. - Do not imply that random assignment is a
146: canonical method of determining a Title.
147: 
148: Guided mode: - Allow the creator to lock a player’s Class, Aspect, or
149: complete Classpect independently. - Randomize only the unassigned
150: components. - Preserve all locked values exactly. - Allow custom Classes
151: or Aspects only when custom content is enabled.
152: 
153: Do not automatically infer a player’s personality, morality, destiny, or
154: behavior from their Classpect.
155: 
156: 3.  SERVER/CLIENT NETWORK
157: 
158: SBURB uses server/client relationships. In this recreation, simulate
159: these relationships as a directed network.
160: 
161: TERMS - Server player: the player who operates the game interface and
162: deploys or manipulates game machinery for another player. - Client
163: player: the player whose game environment is being operated on by their
164: server. - Initial host: the player who begins the session’s game
165: installation/hosting process. This is a session role for the simulation
166: and should not be confused with every later server relationship.
167: 
168: A player may be a client to one player and a server to another. Do not
169: restrict the network to a simple star with one server and many clients.
170: 
171: NETWORK DATA For each player, store: - Their server player’s ID, if
172: assigned. - A list of their client players’ IDs. - Their entry order. -
173: Connection status.
174: 
175: VALIDATION - No player may be their own server. - Connections must
176: reference existing players. - Do not create contradictory or duplicate
177: connections. - The network must not contain an impossible dependency
178: cycle for entry. A player cannot be required to enter before the player
179: whose server assistance is necessary for that entry. - Show the network
180: visually and provide a readable text explanation.
181: 
182: GENERATION Randomized mode: - Generate a valid connected or
183: intentionally partitioned network, depending on the session
184: configuration. - Choose an initial host. - Determine an entry order
185: compatible with the dependency relationships. - If a valid network
186: cannot be produced under the current constraints, explain the conflict
187: and offer to regenerate or relax constraints.
188: 
189: Guided mode: - Let the creator select each player’s server
190: relationship. - Validate the network before generation. - Explain any
191: invalid dependency or cycle and request correction rather than silently
192: changing the network.
193: 
194: Do not assume that every player must have exactly one client or that all
195: sessions must use the same network shape.
196: 
197: 4.  ENTRY SEQUENCE
198: 
199: The entry sequence should be represented as a set of ordered events, not
200: just a single “enter game” button.
201: 
202: CANON ANCHORS The human SBURB entry process involves game machinery
203: including: - Cruxtruder: releases the Cruxite Dowel and initiates a
204: meteor countdown. - Totem Lathe: carves the dowel using a pattern
205: supplied through the entry process. - Alchemiter: produces the Cruxite
206: artifact from the carved dowel. - Kernelsprite: is created/prototyped as
207: part of the entry process. - Cruxite artifact: is used to complete
208: entry.
209: 
210: At a high level, the player and their home are transported into the
211: Medium when the entry artifact is activated/destroyed.
212: 
213: IMPLEMENTATION For each player, track: - Machinery deployed. -
214: Kernelsprite created. - First prototyping completed. - Entry artifact
215: pattern available. - Dowel carved. - Artifact created. - Entry
216: completed. - Meteor countdown state.
217: 
218: The entry screen should communicate which actions are complete and what
219: remains. For the initial generator, it is acceptable to generate an
220: entry plan and status summary rather than fully simulate the machinery
221: interactions.
222: 
223: ENTRY ORDER Entry order must respect the server/client dependency graph.
224: The game should not claim a client can complete a step requiring server
225: deployment before that server has entered or otherwise made the required
226: deployment possible.
227: 
228: 5.  KERNELSPRITES AND PROTOTYPING
229: 
230: Each player receives a Kernelsprite. A Kernelsprite is a guide/companion
231: and is affected by prototyping.
232: 
233: CANON ANCHORS - Prototyping changes the Sprite. - Prototyping has
234: consequences beyond the Sprite itself, including effects on the
235: session’s enemies and the royal powers associated with the game. - The
236: timing of prototyping matters. Pre-entry and post-entry prototyping can
237: have different consequences. - The normal process is associated with two
238: prototyping opportunities, though unusual circumstances can alter
239: events.
240: 
241: PLAYER DATA Each Kernelsprite should record: - Sprite ID. - Owner player
242: ID. - Base appearance/description. - First prototyping input. - First
243: prototyping timing. - Second prototyping input. - Second prototyping
244: timing. - Resulting appearance/personality/abilities. - Session-wide
245: consequences.
246: 
247: GENERATION In guided mode, allow the creator to specify prototyping
248: inputs or leave them random. In randomized mode, generate plausible
249: inputs from a library of objects, creatures, characters, or other
250: entities.
251: 
252: Do not reduce prototyping to a cosmetic adjective or a simple numerical
253: buff. It should create persistent session tags/effects that other
254: systems can inspect.
255: 
256: For the first implementation, create a structured list of prototyping
257: tags and consequences. Keep their exact effects configurable and clearly
258: marked as implementation rules.
259: 
260: 6.  DREAM MOONS
261: 
262: Each player is associated with a dream self on either Prospit or Derse.
263: 
264: CANON ANCHORS - Prospit and Derse are the two dream moons. - A player’s
265: dream self can act and experience events separately from their waking
266: self. - Dream selves and waking selves have distinct states and can be
267: affected separately.
268: 
269: PLAYER DATA - Dream moon. - Dream-self status. - Dream-self location. -
270: Dream-self health/status, if health is implemented. - Relevant dream
271: events.
272: 
273: For the session generator, assign Prospit or Derse either randomly or by
274: creator choice. Do not claim that a simple random assignment is the
275: canonical determination method.
276: 
277: 7.  LAND GENERATION
278: 
279: Every player receives an individual Land in the Medium.
280: 
281: LAND NAME Use the familiar naming format: “Land of [Noun] and [Noun]”
282: 
283: The two defining nouns should be meaningful and evocative. They may
284: describe environmental features, recurring motifs, problems, or thematic
285: ideas. Do not simply concatenate two unrelated random words.
286: 
287: LAND RECORD Each Land should contain: - Unique Land ID. - Owner player
288: ID. - Land name. - Primary environment/biome. - Secondary environment or
289: contrasting feature. - Geography. - Major landmarks. - Settlements. -
290: Consort species and society. - Central problem. - Cause/history of the
291: problem. - Main quest. - Optional quest branches. - Denizen and
292: Denizen’s domain. - Seven Gates and their states. - Enemy/Underling
293: encounter themes. - Resource/grist notes. - Generation rationale
294: connecting the Land to the player’s Aspect and Classpect.
295: 
296: LAND GENERATION LOGIC Generate a coherent combination of: 1. Two Land
297: title nouns. 2. A physical environment. 3. A central problem. 4. A cause
298: for that problem. 5. A quest that addresses the problem. 6. A Denizen
299: and a final challenge. 7. Consorts who have a reason to care about the
300: problem.
301: 
302: Aspect should influence the Land’s motifs and quest, but should not
303: dictate every detail. Classpect may provide additional thematic
304: inspiration. Avoid a simplistic one-to-one mapping such as “all Time
305: players receive clock planets.”
306: 
307: In guided mode, allow the creator to lock one or both title nouns, a
308: biome, a motif, or a quest theme. Generate the remaining details around
309: those constraints.
310: 
311: 8.  CONSORTS AND LAND POPULATIONS
312: 
313: Consorts are native inhabitants of the Lands. They are characters and
314: societies, not merely decorative monsters.
315: 
316: Generate for each Land: - A Consort species or visual archetype. - A
317: short description. - A settlement or society. - Cultural details or
318: customs. - A few named NPCs with distinct roles. - Their understanding
319: of the Land’s central problem. - Quest hooks or information they can
320: provide.
321: 
322: Consort species and societies should be varied. Do not assume all Lands
323: have the same species, culture, or political structure.
324: 
325: NPC records should include: - Name. - Role. - Brief personality or
326: conversational style. - Relevant knowledge. - Quest connection. -
327: Current status.
328: 
329: Do not generate excessive dialogue in the first version. A few useful
330: dialogue options and quest explanations are sufficient.
331: 
332: 9.  DENIZENS
333: 
334: Each Land has a Denizen, an exceptionally powerful entity associated
335: with the Land’s ultimate challenge.
336: 
337: Known examples include Echidna, Typheus, Cetus, and Hephaestus.
338: 
339: DENIZEN RECORD - Name. - Land ID. - Mythological/creature archetype. -
340: Domain or lair. - Temperament. - Connection to the Land’s central
341: problem. - Challenge or trial. - Possible outcomes. - Relevant reward or
342: progression flag.
343: 
344: Do not assume every Denizen is simply a boss that must be killed. The
345: encounter may involve a choice, test, bargain, confrontation, or other
346: resolution.
347: 
348: The Denizen and its challenge should be related to the Land’s quest and
349: the player’s Aspect, without forcing every player into the same kind of
350: encounter.
351: 
352: 10. SEVEN GATES AND LAND PROGRESSION
353: 
354: Each Land has seven Gates forming a progression route toward Skaia.
355: 
356: For the generator, create seven distinct Gate records: - Gate number (1
357: through 7). - Location or landmark. - Requirement to reach or unlock
358: it. - Challenge/obstacle. - Destination or progression effect. -
359: Locked/unlocked/completed status.
360: 
361: The server player’s assistance in constructing and deploying the
362: client’s house is part of the broader progression structure.
363: 
364: Do not invent a detailed universal gate-placement formula and label it
365: canon. Gate placement, obstacles, and unlock conditions may be
366: implementation-generated, provided they are consistent and clearly
367: identified as such.
368: 
369: 11. SESSION-WIDE INITIAL CONDITIONS
370: 
371: The session generator should produce a global session record
372: containing: - Session ID and name. - Generation mode. - Seed. - Player
373: roster. - Server/client graph. - Entry order. - Number of players
374: entered. - Prototyping records. - Initial Battlefield state. - Prospit
375: and Derse state. - Initial meteor countdowns, where relevant. - Session
376: difficulty setting. - Complication level. - Generation warnings and
377: notes.
378: 
379: The Battlefield is affected by player entry and prototyping. The
380: generator should therefore use the roster, entry sequence, and
381: prototyping records when establishing the initial Battlefield state.
382: 
383: Do not treat the Battlefield as an unrelated decorative location. It is
384: part of the session’s shared state.
385: 
386: 12. RANDOMIZED AND GUIDED GENERATION MODES
387: 
388: RANDOMIZED SESSION - The creator supplies only required settings, such
389: as player count and session name. - Generate all remaining values using
390: the session seed. - Produce a complete session overview. - Avoid
391: duplicate Classpects by default when possible, without treating
392: duplicates as invalid. - Generate a valid server/client network and
393: entry order. - Ensure each player receives a coherent Land, Consort
394: population, quest, and Denizen. - Generate prototyping inputs and
395: initial conditions. - Display a summary and allow the creator to inspect
396: each player’s details.
397: 
398: GUIDED SESSION - The creator can lock specific values and leave others
399: unspecified. - Support partial configuration: for example, a creator may
400: specify player names and Classpects while randomizing Lands and
401: connections. - Explicitly locked values must never be overwritten. -
402: Generated values should be designed around the locked values. - Validate
403: dependencies and explain conflicts. - Allow the creator to revise a
404: choice and regenerate only dependent content when practical.
405: 
406: BOTH MODES - Display which values were manually specified and which were
407: generated. - Show the seed. - Allow saving and loading. - Provide a
408: “regenerate” action with clear scope: regenerate the entire session or
409: only a selected section. - If a section is regenerated, preserve locked
410: values and avoid breaking references to other session data.
411: 
412: 13. DATA MODEL AND CODE ORGANIZATION
413: 
414: Use modular JavaScript data structures. Keep definitions separate from
415: generation functions and UI rendering.
416: 
417: Suggested top-level data objects:
418: 
419: Session: - id - name - seed - mode - settings - players[] -
420: connections[] - entryOrder[] - lands[] - battlefield - globalEvents[] -
421: generationLog[]
422: 
423: Player: - id - name - classId - aspectId - title - dreamMoon -
424: serverId - clientIds[] - entryOrder - spriteId - landId - dreamSelf -
425: generationLog[]
426: 
427: Land: - id - ownerId - name - environment - geography - landmarks[] -
428: consorts - quest - denizen - gates[] - resources - enemies -
429: generationLog[]
430: 
431: Sprite: - id - ownerId - prototyping[] - tags[] - description -
432: effects[]
433: 
434: Use stable IDs rather than relying on array positions. Keep a central
435: registry or clearly organized data definitions for Classes, Aspects,
436: Consort archetypes, Land motifs, Denizens, and generation tables.
437: 
438: A seeded random-number generator is strongly preferred. Do not use
439: unrelated calls to Math.random() throughout the code if doing so makes a
440: session impossible to reproduce.
441: 
442: 14. USER INTERFACE REQUIREMENTS
443: 
444: The first playable version should include:
445: 
446: A. Main menu - New Session. - Load Session, if saving is implemented. -
447: Help/Mechanics Reference.
448: 
449: B. Session setup - Randomized or Guided mode. - Player count. - Session
450: name. - Seed. - Optional configuration fields.
451: 
452: C. Player roster - Player cards. - Classpect display. - Dream moon. -
453: Server/client relationship. - Entry order.
454: 
455: D. Session network - A readable visual diagram of server/client
456: relationships. - Clear indication of the initial host. - Validation
457: warnings.
458: 
459: E. Land overview - One card per player. - Land name and environment. -
460: Consort species. - Central quest. - Denizen. - Gate progression.
461: 
462: F. Session summary - Global conditions. - Prototyping consequences. -
463: Battlefield state. - Warnings and unusual circumstances.
464: 
465: The interface should be navigable on a typical desktop browser and
466: remain usable on a mobile screen. Prioritize clarity and functional
467: controls over decorative complexity.
468: 
469: 15. VALIDATION AND QUALITY CHECKS
470: 
471: Before accepting a generated session, validate:
472: 
473: -   Every player has a unique ID.
474: -   Every player has exactly one valid Class and one valid Aspect.
475: -   Every player has one Land.
476: -   Every Land has exactly seven Gate records.
477: -   Every Land has a Consort population.
478: -   Every Land has a Denizen record.
479: -   Every player has a Kernelsprite record.
480: -   Every connection references an existing player.
481: -   No player is their own server.
482: -   Entry dependencies are valid and do not form an impossible cycle.
483: -   Every Land and quest has enough information to be understandable.
484: -   Every generated reference uses a valid ID.
485: -   The seed and generation settings are saved.
486: 
487: If generation fails validation, do not silently display a broken
488: session. Explain the problem and offer regeneration or correction.
489: 
490: 16. OUT OF SCOPE FOR THIS FIRST MILESTONE
491: 
492: Do not attempt to implement all of the following in the initial build: -
493: Full turn-based combat. - Complete enemy stat blocks. - Full Grist
494: economy. - Complete alchemy and every possible item combination. - Fully
495: interactive Sylladex/Fetch Modus system. - Complete Echeladder
496: progression. - Full seven-Gate exploration gameplay. - Complete
497: dream-world exploration. - God Tier ascension. - The Reckoning as a
498: playable real-time event. - Time travel and doomed timelines. - The
499: Scratch. - The Ultimate Alchemy as a complete endgame system. - Actual
500: online multiplayer.
501: 
502: These are future milestones. The first build should focus on producing a
503: coherent session generator with inspectable, interconnected data.
504: 
505: 17. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
506: 
507: The first build is successful if a user can:
508: 
509: 1.  Open the game in a browser.
510: 2.  Start a new human SBURB session.
511: 3.  Select Randomized or Guided generation.
512: 4.  Configure a roster of multiple players.
513: 5.  Generate or specify each player’s Classpect.
514: 6.  Generate or specify a valid server/client network.
515: 7.  Obtain a valid entry order.
516: 8.  Generate a unique Land for each player.
517: 9.  Inspect each Land’s Consorts, quest, Denizen, and seven Gates.
518: 10. Inspect each player’s Kernelsprite and prototyping information.
519: 11. Review the initial session-wide conditions.
520: 12. Save and reopen the generated session, or otherwise preserve its
521:     seed and data.
522: 13. See clear explanations when constraints conflict or generation
523:     fails.
524: 
525: A session should feel like one interconnected game scenario, not a
526: random list of names and descriptions.
527: 
528: 18. INSTRUCTIONS TO THE GAME GENERATOR
529: 
530: Build the first milestone as a functional browser-based application
531: using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
532: 
533: Prioritize a working session-generation flow and reliable data handling.
534: Use modular functions and structured data. Keep content definitions
535: separate from generation logic and UI rendering.
536: 
537: Do not attempt to implement every future SBURB feature now. Do not
538: replace the requested systems with a generic fantasy RPG. Do not invent
539: official canon rules where the comic is ambiguous. Label
540: implementation-specific assumptions.
541: 
542: Make all primary controls functional. Generated data must be internally
543: consistent and visible to the user. Include useful error messages and
544: validation. If a feature cannot be implemented, state that limitation
545: rather than presenting a nonfunctional button.
546: 
547: The deliverable should be a usable first version of the SBURB Session
548: Generator, not merely a static mockup or a description of a proposed
549: game.
550: 
551: END OF SPECIFICATION

## Objective
- Complete the existing browser-based human SBURB session generator from its specification and deliver a coherent, playable, inspectable session flow.

## Requirements
- Support randomized and guided modes, configurable player count, editable seed, and preserve explicit guided choices.
- Generate reproducible, interconnected session data; validate it; support saving/loading and exporting.
- Distinguish canon anchors, interpretations, and implementation rules.
- Provide usable responsive UI with functional controls and avoid implying unimplemented features are functional.
- No clarifying questions; brief assumptions at completion.

## Decisions
- Use modular plain HTML/CSS/JavaScript with seeded generation and a dark responsive console UI.
- Model a valid acyclic server network, entry progression, Lands, Consorts, Denizens, Gates, and descriptive prototyping effects.

3. Run syntax and browser checks, verify seed reproducibility and guided constraints, then report remaining limitations.
