1: SBURB RECREATION PROJECT SESSION GENERATION SPECIFICATION Version 1.0 —
2: 6 November 2026
3: 
4: PURPOSE This document specifies the first major subsystem of a
5: browser-based recreation of human SBURB, inspired by the mechanics and
6: events depicted in Homestuck. It is intended as a handoff document for
7: an AI game-generation tool.
8: 
9: The immediate goal is NOT to implement all of SBURB. The immediate goal
10: is to generate a coherent, inspectable session: its players, Classpects,
11: server/client network, entry order, Lands, Consorts, quests, Denizens,
12: and initial session conditions.
13: 
14: The game should support both fully randomized generation and guided
15: generation in which the creator supplies constraints or fixed choices.
16: 
17: PROJECT DECISIONS — FIXED - Game scope: human SBURB only. Do not
18: implement SGRUB-specific mechanics in this version. - Classpects: use
19: the twelve established Classes and twelve established Aspects as the
20: foundation. Keep the content model extensible for custom Classes,
21: Aspects, and interpretations. - Generation: provide both Randomized
22: Session and Guided Session modes, selectable at session creation. -
23: Multiplayer: simulate multiple players locally; actual online
24: multiplayer is not required. - Platform: browser-based HTML, CSS, and
25: JavaScript. - Development approach: modular and incremental. Preserve
26: working features when extending the game. - Reproducibility: save a
27: session seed and all generated session data so that a session can be
28: reopened and inspected. If practical, allow regeneration from the same
29: seed and configuration.
30: 
31: IMPORTANT CANON POLICY Homestuck does not provide a complete technical
32: manual for every game mechanic. Keep three categories distinct
33: throughout the project:
34: 
35: 1.  CANON ANCHOR: A fact or concept directly established by the comic.
36: 2.  INTERPRETATION: A reasonable reading of material that is
37:     demonstrated but not exhaustively defined.
38: 3.  IMPLEMENTATION RULE: A practical rule invented for this playable
39:     recreation.
40: 
41: Do not label fan interpretations or invented mechanics as official
42: canon. Where a rule is uncertain, mark it as configurable or provisional
43: rather than presenting it as settled fact.
44: 
45: CORE DESIGN PRINCIPLES - Generate a session, not merely a set of
46: unrelated character sheets. - Generated systems must share data.
47: Prototyping should influence session state; player connections should
48: affect entry logistics; Land quests should connect to their Consorts and
49: Denizens. - Guided inputs are constraints. The generator must not
50: silently replace a creator’s explicit choices. - Randomness should be
51: seeded and reproducible. - Generated content should be coherent and
52: explainable. Each generated Land, quest, and complication should have a
53: short explanation of how its pieces relate. - Avoid arbitrary numerical
54: character statistics in this phase. Classpects are thematic identities,
55: not automatically combat classes with canonically defined damage
56: values. - Provide an editable session summary before starting
57: gameplay. - Use readable names, descriptions, and clear controls. The
58: first version should prioritize a functional generator over elaborate
59: graphics.
60: 
61: 1.  SESSION CREATION SCREEN
62: 
63: Provide a New Session flow with the following settings.
64: 
65: REQUIRED SETTINGS - Session name: user-provided or automatically
66: generated. - Generation mode: Randomized Session or Guided Session. -
67: Player count: configurable. Use a sensible default such as four players,
68: but do not hard-code four as the only valid size. - Random seed:
69: automatically generated by default; optionally editable or displayed. -
70: Difficulty: optional implementation setting. Suggested choices: Relaxed,
71: Standard, Challenging, and Severe. These are game-implementation labels,
72: not Homestuck canon categories.
73: 
74: OPTIONAL SETTINGS - Number of players. - Fixed or randomized
75: Classpects. - Fixed or randomized server/client relationships. - Fixed
76: or randomized Prospit/Derse affiliations. - Land themes or environmental
77: preferences. - Desired tone (for example: adventurous, mysterious,
78: eerie, whimsical, or dangerous). - Session complications: disabled,
79: standard, or elevated. - Custom content enabled/disabled.
80: 
81: The creator should be able to leave any optional setting unset. Unset
82: values are generated automatically.
83: 
84: 2.  PLAYER GENERATION
85: 
86: Each player record should contain at least:
87: 
88: -   Unique player ID.
89: -   Display name.
90: -   Optional pronouns or character description, if supplied by the
91:     creator.
92: -   Class.
93: -   Aspect.
94: -   Full Title, formatted as “Class of Aspect”.
95: -   Dream moon: Prospit or Derse.
96: -   Kernelsprite record.
97: -   Server player ID, if any.
98: -   Client player ID(s), if any.
99: -   Entry order.
100: -   Land record ID.
101: -   Generation notes explaining which values were fixed and which were
102:     randomized.
103: 
104: Do not invent personal details such as a player’s personality,
105: appearance, or biography unless the creator asks for character
106: generation. The generator may offer optional personality prompts, but
107: should not overwrite supplied character information.
108: 
109: 2A. CLASSES
110: 
111: The twelve established Classes are: - Heir - Seer - Knight - Page -
112: Mage - Rogue - Thief - Prince - Bard - Maid - Sylph - Witch
113: 
114: Store Class definitions as data rather than embedding them in generation
115: logic. Each definition should support: - Canon name. - Short
116: description. - Longer interpretive description. - Source/status note. -
117: Optional implementation notes. - Custom/official flag.
118: 
119: Class interpretations vary, and the comic does not provide a complete
120: ability specification for every Class. Do not generate definitive canon
121: ability trees. For this stage, a Class supplies a thematic description
122: and may later inform ability design.
123: 
124: 2B. ASPECTS
125: 
126: The twelve established Aspects are: - Time - Space - Light - Void -
127: Heart - Mind - Rage - Hope - Life - Doom - Breath - Blood
128: 
129: Store Aspect definitions as data. Each should support: - Canon name. -
130: Core thematic keywords. - Short description. - Longer interpretive
131: description. - Source/status note. - Optional implementation notes. -
132: Custom/official flag.
133: 
134: The keywords and descriptions should be treated as thematic guides, not
135: exhaustive mechanical definitions.
136: 
137: 2C. CLASSPECT ASSIGNMENT
138: 
139: A standard Classpect consists of one Class and one Aspect. The
140: twelve-by-twelve foundation provides 144 possible combinations.
141: 
142: Randomized mode: - Select one valid Class and one valid Aspect for each
143: player. - Avoid duplicate Classpects by default when enough combinations
144: are available, but do not prohibit duplicates unless the creator enables
145: a uniqueness setting. - Do not imply that random assignment is a
146: canonical method of determining a Title.
147: 
148: Guided mode: - Allow the creator to lock a player’s Class, Aspect, or
149: complete Classpect independently. - Randomize only the unassigned
150: components. - Preserve all locked values exactly. - Allow custom Classes
151: or Aspects only when custom content is enabled.
152: 
153: Do not automatically infer a player’s personality, morality, destiny, or
154: behavior from their Classpect.
155: 
156: 3.  SERVER/CLIENT NETWORK
157: 
158: SBURB uses server/client relationships. In this recreation, simulate
159: these relationships as a directed network.
160: 
161: TERMS - Server player: the player who operates the game interface and
162: deploys or manipulates game machinery for another player. - Client
163: player: the player whose game environment is being operated on by their
164: server. - Initial host: the player who begins the session’s game
165: installation/hosting process. This is a session role for the simulation
166: and should not be confused with every later server relationship.
167: 
168: A player may be a client to one player and a server to another. Do not
169: restrict the network to a simple star with one server and many clients.
170: 
171: NETWORK DATA For each player, store: - Their server player’s ID, if
172: assigned. - A list of their client players’ IDs. - Their entry order. -
173: Connection status.
174: 
175: VALIDATION - No player may be their own server. - Connections must
176: reference existing players. - Do not create contradictory or duplicate
177: connections. - The network must not contain an impossible dependency
178: cycle for entry. A player cannot be required to enter before the player
179: whose server assistance is necessary for that entry. - Show the network
180: visually and provide a readable text explanation.
181: 
182: GENERATION Randomized mode: - Generate a valid connected or
183: intentionally partitioned network, depending on the session
184: configuration. - Choose an initial host. - Determine an entry order
185: compatible with the dependency relationships. - If a valid network
186: cannot be produced under the current constraints, explain the conflict
187: and offer to regenerate or relax constraints.
188: 
189: Guided mode: - Let the creator select each player’s server
190: relationship. - Validate the network before generation. - Explain any
191: invalid dependency or cycle and request correction rather than silently
192: changing the network.
193: 
194: Do not assume that every player must have exactly one client or that all
195: sessions must use the same network shape.
196: 
197: 4.  ENTRY SEQUENCE
198: 
199: The entry sequence should be represented as a set of ordered events, not
200: just a single “enter game” button.
201: 
202: CANON ANCHORS The human SBURB entry process involves game machinery
203: including: - Cruxtruder: releases the Cruxite Dowel and initiates a
204: meteor countdown. - Totem Lathe: carves the dowel using a pattern
205: supplied through the entry process. - Alchemiter: produces the Cruxite
206: artifact from the carved dowel. - Kernelsprite: is created/prototyped as
207: part of the entry process. - Cruxite artifact: is used to complete
208: entry.
209: 
210: At a high level, the player and their home are transported into the
211: Medium when the entry artifact is activated/destroyed.
212: 
213: IMPLEMENTATION For each player, track: - Machinery deployed. -
214: Kernelsprite created. - First prototyping completed. - Entry artifact
215: pattern available. - Dowel carved. - Artifact created. - Entry
216: completed. - Meteor countdown state.
217: 
218: The entry screen should communicate which actions are complete and what
219: remains. For the initial generator, it is acceptable to generate an
220: entry plan and status summary rather than fully simulate the machinery
221: interactions.
222: 
223: ENTRY ORDER Entry order must respect the server/client dependency graph.
224: The game should not claim a client can complete a step requiring server
225: deployment before that server has entered or otherwise made the required
226: deployment possible.
227: 
228: 5.  KERNELSPRITES AND PROTOTYPING
229: 
230: Each player receives a Kernelsprite. A Kernelsprite is a guide/companion
231: and is affected by prototyping.
232: 
233: CANON ANCHORS - Prototyping changes the Sprite. - Prototyping has
234: consequences beyond the Sprite itself, including effects on the
235: session’s enemies and the royal powers associated with the game. - The
236: timing of prototyping matters. Pre-entry and post-entry prototyping can
237: have different consequences. - The normal process is associated with two
238: prototyping opportunities, though unusual circumstances can alter
239: events.
240: 
241: PLAYER DATA Each Kernelsprite should record: - Sprite ID. - Owner player
242: ID. - Base appearance/description. - First prototyping input. - First
243: prototyping timing. - Second prototyping input. - Second prototyping
244: timing. - Resulting appearance/personality/abilities. - Session-wide
245: consequences.
246: 
247: GENERATION In guided mode, allow the creator to specify prototyping
248: inputs or leave them random. In randomized mode, generate plausible
249: inputs from a library of objects, creatures, characters, or other
250: entities.
251: 
252: Do not reduce prototyping to a cosmetic adjective or a simple numerical
253: buff. It should create persistent session tags/effects that other
254: systems can inspect.
255: 
256: For the first implementation, create a structured list of prototyping
257: tags and consequences. Keep their exact effects configurable and clearly
258: marked as implementation rules.
259: 
260: 6.  DREAM MOONS
261: 
262: Each player is associated with a dream self on either Prospit or Derse.
263: 
264: CANON ANCHORS - Prospit and Derse are the two dream moons. - A player’s
265: dream self can act and experience events separately from their waking
266: self. - Dream selves and waking selves have distinct states and can be
267: affected separately.
268: 
269: PLAYER DATA - Dream moon. - Dream-self status. - Dream-self location. -
270: Dream-self health/status, if health is implemented. - Relevant dream
271: events.
272: 
273: For the session generator, assign Prospit or Derse either randomly or by
274: creator choice. Do not claim that a simple random assignment is the
275: canonical determination method.
276: 
277: 7.  LAND GENERATION
278: 
279: Every player receives an individual Land in the Medium.
280: 
281: LAND NAME Use the familiar naming format: “Land of [Noun] and [Noun]”
282: 
283: The two defining nouns should be meaningful and evocative. They may
284: describe environmental features, recurring motifs, problems, or thematic
285: ideas. Do not simply concatenate two unrelated random words.
286: 
287: LAND RECORD Each Land should contain: - Unique Land ID. - Owner player
288: ID. - Land name. - Primary environment/biome. - Secondary environment or
289: contrasting feature. - Geography. - Major landmarks. - Settlements. -
290: Consort species and society. - Central problem. - Cause/history of the
291: problem. - Main quest. - Optional quest branches. - Denizen and
292: Denizen’s domain. - Seven Gates and their states. - Enemy/Underling
293: encounter themes. - Resource/grist notes. - Generation rationale
294: connecting the Land to the player’s Aspect and Classpect.
295: 
296: LAND GENERATION LOGIC Generate a coherent combination of: 1. Two Land
297: title nouns. 2. A physical environment. 3. A central problem. 4. A cause
298: for that problem. 5. A quest that addresses the problem. 6. A Denizen
299: and a final challenge. 7. Consorts who have a reason to care about the
300: problem.
301: 
302: Aspect should influence the Land’s motifs and quest, but should not
303: dictate every detail. Classpect may provide additional thematic
304: inspiration. Avoid a simplistic one-to-one mapping such as “all Time
305: players receive clock planets.”
306: 
307: In guided mode, allow the creator to lock one or both title nouns, a
308: biome, a motif, or a quest theme. Generate the remaining details around
309: those constraints.
310: 
311: 8.  CONSORTS AND LAND POPULATIONS
312: 
313: Consorts are native inhabitants of the Lands. They are characters and
314: societies, not merely decorative monsters.
315: 
316: Generate for each Land: - A Consort species or visual archetype. - A
317: short description. - A settlement or society. - Cultural details or
318: customs. - A few named NPCs with distinct roles. - Their understanding
319: of the Land’s central problem. - Quest hooks or information they can
320: provide.
321: 
322: Consort species and societies should be varied. Do not assume all Lands
323: have the same species, culture, or political structure.
324: 
325: NPC records should include: - Name. - Role. - Brief personality or
326: conversational style. - Relevant knowledge. - Quest connection. -
327: Current status.
328: 
329: Do not generate excessive dialogue in the first version. A few useful
330: dialogue options and quest explanations are sufficient.
331: 
332: 9.  DENIZENS
333: 
334: Each Land has a Denizen, an exceptionally powerful entity associated
335: with the Land’s ultimate challenge.
336: 
337: Known examples include Echidna, Typheus, Cetus, and Hephaestus.
338: 
339: DENIZEN RECORD - Name. - Land ID. - Mythological/creature archetype. -
340: Domain or lair. - Temperament. - Connection to the Land’s central
341: problem. - Challenge or trial. - Possible outcomes. - Relevant reward or
342: progression flag.
343: 
344: Do not assume every Denizen is simply a boss that must be killed. The
345: encounter may involve a choice, test, bargain, confrontation, or other
346: resolution.
347: 
348: The Denizen and its challenge should be related to the Land’s quest and
349: the player’s Aspect, without forcing every player into the same kind of
350: encounter.
351: 
352: 10. SEVEN GATES AND LAND PROGRESSION
353: 
354: Each Land has seven Gates forming a progression route toward Skaia.
355: 
356: For the generator, create seven distinct Gate records: - Gate number (1
357: through 7). - Location or landmark. - Requirement to reach or unlock
358: it. - Challenge/obstacle. - Destination or progression effect. -
359: Locked/unlocked/completed status.
360: 
361: The server player’s assistance in constructing and deploying the
362: client’s house is part of the broader progression structure.
363: 
364: Do not invent a detailed universal gate-placement formula and label it
365: canon. Gate placement, obstacles, and unlock conditions may be
366: implementation-generated, provided they are consistent and clearly
367: identified as such.
368: 
369: 11. SESSION-WIDE INITIAL CONDITIONS
370: 
371: The session generator should produce a global session record
372: containing: - Session ID and name. - Generation mode. - Seed. - Player
373: roster. - Server/client graph. - Entry order. - Number of players
374: entered. - Prototyping records. - Initial Battlefield state. - Prospit
375: and Derse state. - Initial meteor countdowns, where relevant. - Session
376: difficulty setting. - Complication level. - Generation warnings and
377: notes.
378: 
379: The Battlefield is affected by player entry and prototyping. The
380: generator should therefore use the roster, entry sequence, and
381: prototyping records when establishing the initial Battlefield state.
382: 
383: Do not treat the Battlefield as an unrelated decorative location. It is
384: part of the session’s shared state.
385: 
386: 12. RANDOMIZED AND GUIDED GENERATION MODES
387: 
388: RANDOMIZED SESSION - The creator supplies only required settings, such
389: as player count and session name. - Generate all remaining values using
390: the session seed. - Produce a complete session overview. - Avoid
391: duplicate Classpects by default when possible, without treating
392: duplicates as invalid. - Generate a valid server/client network and
393: entry order. - Ensure each player receives a coherent Land, Consort
394: population, quest, and Denizen. - Generate prototyping inputs and
395: initial conditions. - Display a summary and allow the creator to inspect
396: each player’s details.
397: 
398: GUIDED SESSION - The creator can lock specific values and leave others
399: unspecified. - Support partial configuration: for example, a creator may
400: specify player names and Classpects while randomizing Lands and
401: connections. - Explicitly locked values must never be overwritten. -
402: Generated values should be designed around the locked values. - Validate
403: dependencies and explain conflicts. - Allow the creator to revise a
404: choice and regenerate only dependent content when practical.
405: 
406: BOTH MODES - Display which values were manually specified and which were
407: generated. - Show the seed. - Allow saving and loading. - Provide a
408: “regenerate” action with clear scope: regenerate the entire session or
409: only a selected section. - If a section is regenerated, preserve locked
410: values and avoid breaking references to other session data.
411: 
412: 13. DATA MODEL AND CODE ORGANIZATION
413: 
414: Use modular JavaScript data structures. Keep definitions separate from
415: generation functions and UI rendering.
416: 
417: Suggested top-level data objects:
418: 
419: Session: - id - name - seed - mode - settings - players[] -
420: connections[] - entryOrder[] - lands[] - battlefield - globalEvents[] -
421: generationLog[]
422: 
423: Player: - id - name - classId - aspectId - title - dreamMoon -
424: serverId - clientIds[] - entryOrder - spriteId - landId - dreamSelf -
425: generationLog[]
426: 
427: Land: - id - ownerId - name - environment - geography - landmarks[] -
428: consorts - quest - denizen - gates[] - resources - enemies -
429: generationLog[]
430: 
431: Sprite: - id - ownerId - prototyping[] - tags[] - description -
432: effects[]
433: 
434: Use stable IDs rather than relying on array positions. Keep a central
435: registry or clearly organized data definitions for Classes, Aspects,
436: Consort archetypes, Land motifs, Denizens, and generation tables.
437: 
438: A seeded random-number generator is strongly preferred. Do not use
439: unrelated calls to Math.random() throughout the code if doing so makes a
440: session impossible to reproduce.
441: 
442: 14. USER INTERFACE REQUIREMENTS
443: 
444: The first playable version should include:
445: 
446: A. Main menu - New Session. - Load Session, if saving is implemented. -
447: Help/Mechanics Reference.
448: 
449: B. Session setup - Randomized or Guided mode. - Player count. - Session
450: name. - Seed. - Optional configuration fields.
451: 
452: C. Player roster - Player cards. - Classpect display. - Dream moon. -
453: Server/client relationship. - Entry order.
454: 
455: D. Session network - A readable visual diagram of server/client
456: relationships. - Clear indication of the initial host. - Validation
457: warnings.
458: 
459: E. Land overview - One card per player. - Land name and environment. -
460: Consort species. - Central quest. - Denizen. - Gate progression.
461: 
462: F. Session summary - Global conditions. - Prototyping consequences. -
463: Battlefield state. - Warnings and unusual circumstances.
464: 
465: The interface should be navigable on a typical desktop browser and
466: remain usable on a mobile screen. Prioritize clarity and functional
467: controls over decorative complexity.
468: 
469: 15. VALIDATION AND QUALITY CHECKS
470: 
471: Before accepting a generated session, validate:
472: 
473: -   Every player has a unique ID.
474: -   Every player has exactly one valid Class and one valid Aspect.
475: -   Every player has one Land.
476: -   Every Land has exactly seven Gate records.
477: -   Every Land has a Consort population.
478: -   Every Land has a Denizen record.
479: -   Every player has a Kernelsprite record.
480: -   Every connection references an existing player.
481: -   No player is their own server.
482: -   Entry dependencies are valid and do not form an impossible cycle.
483: -   Every Land and quest has enough information to be understandable.
484: -   Every generated reference uses a valid ID.
485: -   The seed and generation settings are saved.
486: 
487: If generation fails validation, do not silently display a broken
488: session. Explain the problem and offer regeneration or correction.
489: 
490: 16. OUT OF SCOPE FOR THIS FIRST MILESTONE
491: 
492: Do not attempt to implement all of the following in the initial build: -
493: Full turn-based combat. - Complete enemy stat blocks. - Full Grist
494: economy. - Complete alchemy and every possible item combination. - Fully
495: interactive Sylladex/Fetch Modus system. - Complete Echeladder
496: progression. - Full seven-Gate exploration gameplay. - Complete
497: dream-world exploration. - God Tier ascension. - The Reckoning as a
498: playable real-time event. - Time travel and doomed timelines. - The
499: Scratch. - The Ultimate Alchemy as a complete endgame system. - Actual
500: online multiplayer.
501: 
502: These are future milestones. The first build should focus on producing a
503: coherent session generator with inspectable, interconnected data.
504: 
505: 17. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
506: 
507: The first build is successful if a user can:
508: 
509: 1.  Open the game in a browser.
510: 2.  Start a new human SBURB session.
511: 3.  Select Randomized or Guided generation.
512: 4.  Configure a roster of multiple players.
513: 5.  Generate or specify each player’s Classpect.
514: 6.  Generate or specify a valid server/client network.
515: 7.  Obtain a valid entry order.
516: 8.  Generate a unique Land for each player.
517: 9.  Inspect each Land’s Consorts, quest, Denizen, and seven Gates.
518: 10. Inspect each player’s Kernelsprite and prototyping information.
519: 11. Review the initial session-wide conditions.
520: 12. Save and reopen the generated session, or otherwise preserve its
521:     seed and data.
522: 13. See clear explanations when constraints conflict or generation
523:     fails.
524: 
525: A session should feel like one interconnected game scenario, not a
526: random list of names and descriptions.
527: 
528: 18. INSTRUCTIONS TO THE GAME GENERATOR
529: 
530: Build the first milestone as a functional browser-based application
531: using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
532: 
533: Prioritize a working session-generation flow and reliable data handling.
534: Use modular functions and structured data. Keep content definitions
535: separate from generation logic and UI rendering.
536: 
537: Do not attempt to implement every future SBURB feature now. Do not
538: replace the requested systems with a generic fantasy RPG. Do not invent
539: official canon rules where the comic is ambiguous. Label
540: implementation-specific assumptions.
541: 
542: Make all primary controls functional. Generated data must be internally
543: consistent and visible to the user. Include useful error messages and
544: validation. If a feature cannot be implemented, state that limitation
545: rather than presenting a nonfunctional button.
546: 
547: The deliverable should be a usable first version of the SBURB Session
548: Generator, not merely a static mockup or a description of a proposed
549: game.
550: 
551: END OF SPECIFICATION

## Objective
- Complete the browser-based human SBURB session generator into a coherent, playable, inspectable session flow.

## Requirements
- Support randomized and guided modes, configurable player count, editable seed, and preserve explicit guided choices.
- Generate reproducible, interconnected session data; validate it; support saving/loading and exporting.
- Distinguish canon anchors, interpretations, and implementation rules.
- Provide usable responsive UI with functional controls and avoid implying unimplemented features are functional.
- No clarifying questions; brief assumptions at completion.

## Decisions
- Use modular plain HTML/CSS/JavaScript with seeded generation and a dark responsive console UI.
- Model an acyclic server network, entry progression, Lands, Consorts, Denizens, Gates, and descriptive prototyping effects.

## Work State
### Completed
- Retrieved and reviewed the specification at `https://omgithub.com/api/issue-attachments/ae9b3937-7d69-4d81-9983-e2ebd2f58f10`.
- Reviewed existing `index.html` and `style.css`.
- `app.js` includes generation and validation logic, plus renderers for overview, players, network, Lands, entry, reference, and a session render function.
- Added network topological validation/reordering logic in `commitNetwork()`.

### Active
- Finish `app.js`: wire setup and navigation, entry progression, Gate actions, save/load/import/export, dialogs, and initialization.
- Parse/test the app, verify setup-to-session flow, seed reproducibility and guided constraints, then inspect in browser.

### Blocked
- `app.js` currently ends at `commitNetwork()` without event handlers, initialization, or the closing IIFE; the application is not yet runnable as a complete experience.

## Next Move
1. Inspect the current `app.js` and complete its missing handlers and initialization.
2. Implement guided setup, tabs, entry/Gate actions, persistence/import/export, and error/toast handling.
3. Run syntax and browser checks; fix issues and report any remaining limitations.

## Relevant Files
- `app.js`: Main implementation; currently incomplete.
- `index.html`: App structure and DOM hooks.
- `style.css`: Existing UI and responsive styling.
- `/tmp/opencode/SBurb_Session_Generation_Specification.txt`: Complete project specification.

## Important Context
- Changes are uncommitted.
- Generation currently creates an acyclic server graph, topologically orders players, and validates player/Land/Sprite references and Gate counts.
- Recent edits appended the renderers and `commitNetwork()` successfully; an attempted edit afterward made no changes.

1: SBURB RECREATION PROJECT SESSION GENERATION SPECIFICATION Version 1.0 —
2: 6 November 2026
3: 
4: PURPOSE This document specifies the first major subsystem of a
5: browser-based recreation of human SBURB, inspired by the mechanics and
6: events depicted in Homestuck. It is intended as a handoff document for
7: an AI game-generation tool.
8: 
9: The immediate goal is NOT to implement all of SBURB. The immediate goal
10: is to generate a coherent, inspectable session: its players, Classpects,
11: server/client network, entry order, Lands, Consorts, quests, Denizens,
12: and initial session conditions.
13: 
14: The game should support both fully randomized generation and guided
15: generation in which the creator supplies constraints or fixed choices.
16: 
17: PROJECT DECISIONS — FIXED - Game scope: human SBURB only. Do not
18: implement SGRUB-specific mechanics in this version. - Classpects: use
19: the twelve established Classes and twelve established Aspects as the
20: foundation. Keep the content model extensible for custom Classes,
21: Aspects, and interpretations. - Generation: provide both Randomized
22: Session and Guided Session modes, selectable at session creation. -
23: Multiplayer: simulate multiple players locally; actual online
24: multiplayer is not required. - Platform: browser-based HTML, CSS, and
25: JavaScript. - Development approach: modular and incremental. Preserve
26: working features when extending the game. - Reproducibility: save a
27: session seed and all generated session data so that a session can be
28: reopened and inspected. If practical, allow regeneration from the same
29: seed and configuration.
30: 
31: IMPORTANT CANON POLICY Homestuck does not provide a complete technical
32: manual for every game mechanic. Keep three categories distinct
33: throughout the project:
34: 
35: 1.  CANON ANCHOR: A fact or concept directly established by the comic.
36: 2.  INTERPRETATION: A reasonable reading of material that is
37:     demonstrated but not exhaustively defined.
38: 3.  IMPLEMENTATION RULE: A practical rule invented for this playable
39:     recreation.
40: 
41: Do not label fan interpretations or invented mechanics as official
42: canon. Where a rule is uncertain, mark it as configurable or provisional
43: rather than presenting it as settled fact.
44: 
45: CORE DESIGN PRINCIPLES - Generate a session, not merely a set of
46: unrelated character sheets. - Generated systems must share data.
47: Prototyping should influence session state; player connections should
48: affect entry logistics; Land quests should connect to their Consorts and
49: Denizens. - Guided inputs are constraints. The generator must not
50: silently replace a creator’s explicit choices. - Randomness should be
51: seeded and reproducible. - Generated content should be coherent and
52: explainable. Each generated Land, quest, and complication should have a
53: short explanation of how its pieces relate. - Avoid arbitrary numerical
54: character statistics in this phase. Classpects are thematic identities,
55: not automatically combat classes with canonically defined damage
56: values. - Provide an editable session summary before starting
57: gameplay. - Use readable names, descriptions, and clear controls. The
58: first version should prioritize a functional generator over elaborate
59: graphics.
60: 
61: 1.  SESSION CREATION SCREEN
62: 
63: Provide a New Session flow with the following settings.
64: 
65: REQUIRED SETTINGS - Session name: user-provided or automatically
66: generated. - Generation mode: Randomized Session or Guided Session. -
67: Player count: configurable. Use a sensible default such as four players,
68: but do not hard-code four as the only valid size. - Random seed:
69: automatically generated by default; optionally editable or displayed. -
70: Difficulty: optional implementation setting. Suggested choices: Relaxed,
71: Standard, Challenging, and Severe. These are game-implementation labels,
72: not Homestuck canon categories.
73: 
74: OPTIONAL SETTINGS - Number of players. - Fixed or randomized
75: Classpects. - Fixed or randomized server/client relationships. - Fixed
76: or randomized Prospit/Derse affiliations. - Land themes or environmental
77: preferences. - Desired tone (for example: adventurous, mysterious,
78: eerie, whimsical, or dangerous). - Session complications: disabled,
79: standard, or elevated. - Custom content enabled/disabled.
80: 
81: The creator should be able to leave any optional setting unset. Unset
82: values are generated automatically.
83: 
84: 2.  PLAYER GENERATION
85: 
86: Each player record should contain at least:
87: 
88: -   Unique player ID.
89: -   Display name.
90: -   Optional pronouns or character description, if supplied by the
91:     creator.
92: -   Class.
93: -   Aspect.
94: -   Full Title, formatted as “Class of Aspect”.
95: -   Dream moon: Prospit or Derse.
96: -   Kernelsprite record.
97: -   Server player ID, if any.
98: -   Client player ID(s), if any.
99: -   Entry order.
100: -   Land record ID.
101: -   Generation notes explaining which values were fixed and which were
102:     randomized.
103: 
104: Do not invent personal details such as a player’s personality,
105: appearance, or biography unless the creator asks for character
106: generation. The generator may offer optional personality prompts, but
107: should not overwrite supplied character information.
108: 
109: 2A. CLASSES
110: 
111: The twelve established Classes are: - Heir - Seer - Knight - Page -
112: Mage - Rogue - Thief - Prince - Bard - Maid - Sylph - Witch
113: 
114: Store Class definitions as data rather than embedding them in generation
115: logic. Each definition should support: - Canon name. - Short
116: description. - Longer interpretive description. - Source/status note. -
117: Optional implementation notes. - Custom/official flag.
118: 
119: Class interpretations vary, and the comic does not provide a complete
120: ability specification for every Class. Do not generate definitive canon
121: ability trees. For this stage, a Class supplies a thematic description
122: and may later inform ability design.
123: 
124: 2B. ASPECTS
125: 
126: The twelve established Aspects are: - Time - Space - Light - Void -
127: Heart - Mind - Rage - Hope - Life - Doom - Breath - Blood
128: 
129: Store Aspect definitions as data. Each should support: - Canon name. -
130: Core thematic keywords. - Short description. - Longer interpretive
131: description. - Source/status note. - Optional implementation notes. -
132: Custom/official flag.
133: 
134: The keywords and descriptions should be treated as thematic guides, not
135: exhaustive mechanical definitions.
136: 
137: 2C. CLASSPECT ASSIGNMENT
138: 
139: A standard Classpect consists of one Class and one Aspect. The
140: twelve-by-twelve foundation provides 144 possible combinations.
141: 
142: Randomized mode: - Select one valid Class and one valid Aspect for each
143: player. - Avoid duplicate Classpects by default when enough combinations
144: are available, but do not prohibit duplicates unless the creator enables
145: a uniqueness setting. - Do not imply that random assignment is a
146: canonical method of determining a Title.
147: 
148: Guided mode: - Allow the creator to lock a player’s Class, Aspect, or
149: complete Classpect independently. - Randomize only the unassigned
150: components. - Preserve all locked values exactly. - Allow custom Classes
151: or Aspects only when custom content is enabled.
152: 
153: Do not automatically infer a player’s personality, morality, destiny, or
154: behavior from their Classpect.
155: 
156: 3.  SERVER/CLIENT NETWORK
157: 
158: SBURB uses server/client relationships. In this recreation, simulate
159: these relationships as a directed network.
160: 
161: TERMS - Server player: the player who operates the game interface and
162: deploys or manipulates game machinery for another player. - Client
163: player: the player whose game environment is being operated on by their
164: server. - Initial host: the player who begins the session’s game
165: installation/hosting process. This is a session role for the simulation
166: and should not be confused with every later server relationship.
167: 
168: A player may be a client to one player and a server to another. Do not
169: restrict the network to a simple star with one server and many clients.
170: 
171: NETWORK DATA For each player, store: - Their server player’s ID, if
172: assigned. - A list of their client players’ IDs. - Their entry order. -
173: Connection status.
174: 
175: VALIDATION - No player may be their own server. - Connections must
176: reference existing players. - Do not create contradictory or duplicate
177: connections. - The network must not contain an impossible dependency
178: cycle for entry. A player cannot be required to enter before the player
179: whose server assistance is necessary for that entry. - Show the network
180: visually and provide a readable text explanation.
181: 
182: GENERATION Randomized mode: - Generate a valid connected or
183: intentionally partitioned network, depending on the session
184: configuration. - Choose an initial host. - Determine an entry order
185: compatible with the dependency relationships. - If a valid network
186: cannot be produced under the current constraints, explain the conflict
187: and offer to regenerate or relax constraints.
188: 
189: Guided mode: - Let the creator select each player’s server
190: relationship. - Validate the network before generation. - Explain any
191: invalid dependency or cycle and request correction rather than silently
192: changing the network.
193: 
194: Do not assume that every player must have exactly one client or that all
195: sessions must use the same network shape.
196: 
197: 4.  ENTRY SEQUENCE
198: 
199: The entry sequence should be represented as a set of ordered events, not
200: just a single “enter game” button.
201: 
202: CANON ANCHORS The human SBURB entry process involves game machinery
203: including: - Cruxtruder: releases the Cruxite Dowel and initiates a
204: meteor countdown. - Totem Lathe: carves the dowel using a pattern
205: supplied through the entry process. - Alchemiter: produces the Cruxite
206: artifact from the carved dowel. - Kernelsprite: is created/prototyped as
207: part of the entry process. - Cruxite artifact: is used to complete
208: entry.
209: 
210: At a high level, the player and their home are transported into the
211: Medium when the entry artifact is activated/destroyed.
212: 
213: IMPLEMENTATION For each player, track: - Machinery deployed. -
214: Kernelsprite created. - First prototyping completed. - Entry artifact
215: pattern available. - Dowel carved. - Artifact created. - Entry
216: completed. - Meteor countdown state.
217: 
218: The entry screen should communicate which actions are complete and what
219: remains. For the initial generator, it is acceptable to generate an
220: entry plan and status summary rather than fully simulate the machinery
221: interactions.
222: 
223: ENTRY ORDER Entry order must respect the server/client dependency graph.
224: The game should not claim a client can complete a step requiring server
225: deployment before that server has entered or otherwise made the required
226: deployment possible.
227: 
228: 5.  KERNELSPRITES AND PROTOTYPING
229: 
230: Each player receives a Kernelsprite. A Kernelsprite is a guide/companion
231: and is affected by prototyping.
232: 
233: CANON ANCHORS - Prototyping changes the Sprite. - Prototyping has
234: consequences beyond the Sprite itself, including effects on the
235: session’s enemies and the royal powers associated with the game. - The
236: timing of prototyping matters. Pre-entry and post-entry prototyping can
237: have different consequences. - The normal process is associated with two
238: prototyping opportunities, though unusual circumstances can alter
239: events.
240: 
241: PLAYER DATA Each Kernelsprite should record: - Sprite ID. - Owner player
242: ID. - Base appearance/description. - First prototyping input. - First
243: prototyping timing. - Second prototyping input. - Second prototyping
244: timing. - Resulting appearance/personality/abilities. - Session-wide
245: consequences.
246: 
247: GENERATION In guided mode, allow the creator to specify prototyping
248: inputs or leave them random. In randomized mode, generate plausible
249: inputs from a library of objects, creatures, characters, or other
250: entities.
251: 
252: Do not reduce prototyping to a cosmetic adjective or a simple numerical
253: buff. It should create persistent session tags/effects that other
254: systems can inspect.
255: 
256: For the first implementation, create a structured list of prototyping
257: tags and consequences. Keep their exact effects configurable and clearly
258: marked as implementation rules.
259: 
260: 6.  DREAM MOONS
261: 
262: Each player is associated with a dream self on either Prospit or Derse.
263: 
264: CANON ANCHORS - Prospit and Derse are the two dream moons. - A player’s
265: dream self can act and experience events separately from their waking
266: self. - Dream selves and waking selves have distinct states and can be
267: affected separately.
268: 
269: PLAYER DATA - Dream moon. - Dream-self status. - Dream-self location. -
270: Dream-self health/status, if health is implemented. - Relevant dream
271: events.
272: 
273: For the session generator, assign Prospit or Derse either randomly or by
274: creator choice. Do not claim that a simple random assignment is the
275: canonical determination method.
276: 
277: 7.  LAND GENERATION
278: 
279: Every player receives an individual Land in the Medium.
280: 
281: LAND NAME Use the familiar naming format: “Land of [Noun] and [Noun]”
282: 
283: The two defining nouns should be meaningful and evocative. They may
284: describe environmental features, recurring motifs, problems, or thematic
285: ideas. Do not simply concatenate two unrelated random words.
286: 
287: LAND RECORD Each Land should contain: - Unique Land ID. - Owner player
288: ID. - Land name. - Primary environment/biome. - Secondary environment or
289: contrasting feature. - Geography. - Major landmarks. - Settlements. -
290: Consort species and society. - Central problem. - Cause/history of the
291: problem. - Main quest. - Optional quest branches. - Denizen and
292: Denizen’s domain. - Seven Gates and their states. - Enemy/Underling
293: encounter themes. - Resource/grist notes. - Generation rationale
294: connecting the Land to the player’s Aspect and Classpect.
295: 
296: LAND GENERATION LOGIC Generate a coherent combination of: 1. Two Land
297: title nouns. 2. A physical environment. 3. A central problem. 4. A cause
298: for that problem. 5. A quest that addresses the problem. 6. A Denizen
299: and a final challenge. 7. Consorts who have a reason to care about the
300: problem.
301: 
302: Aspect should influence the Land’s motifs and quest, but should not
303: dictate every detail. Classpect may provide additional thematic
304: inspiration. Avoid a simplistic one-to-one mapping such as “all Time
305: players receive clock planets.”
306: 
307: In guided mode, allow the creator to lock one or both title nouns, a
308: biome, a motif, or a quest theme. Generate the remaining details around
309: those constraints.
310: 
311: 8.  CONSORTS AND LAND POPULATIONS
312: 
313: Consorts are native inhabitants of the Lands. They are characters and
314: societies, not merely decorative monsters.
315: 
316: Generate for each Land: - A Consort species or visual archetype. - A
317: short description. - A settlement or society. - Cultural details or
318: customs. - A few named NPCs with distinct roles. - Their understanding
319: of the Land’s central problem. - Quest hooks or information they can
320: provide.
321: 
322: Consort species and societies should be varied. Do not assume all Lands
323: have the same species, culture, or political structure.
324: 
325: NPC records should include: - Name. - Role. - Brief personality or
326: conversational style. - Relevant knowledge. - Quest connection. -
327: Current status.
328: 
329: Do not generate excessive dialogue in the first version. A few useful
330: dialogue options and quest explanations are sufficient.
331: 
332: 9.  DENIZENS
333: 
334: Each Land has a Denizen, an exceptionally powerful entity associated
335: with the Land’s ultimate challenge.
336: 
337: Known examples include Echidna, Typheus, Cetus, and Hephaestus.
338: 
339: DENIZEN RECORD - Name. - Land ID. - Mythological/creature archetype. -
340: Domain or lair. - Temperament. - Connection to the Land’s central
341: problem. - Challenge or trial. - Possible outcomes. - Relevant reward or
342: progression flag.
343: 
344: Do not assume every Denizen is simply a boss that must be killed. The
345: encounter may involve a choice, test, bargain, confrontation, or other
346: resolution.
347: 
348: The Denizen and its challenge should be related to the Land’s quest and
349: the player’s Aspect, without forcing every player into the same kind of
350: encounter.
351: 
352: 10. SEVEN GATES AND LAND PROGRESSION
353: 
354: Each Land has seven Gates forming a progression route toward Skaia.
355: 
356: For the generator, create seven distinct Gate records: - Gate number (1
357: through 7). - Location or landmark. - Requirement to reach or unlock
358: it. - Challenge/obstacle. - Destination or progression effect. -
359: Locked/unlocked/completed status.
360: 
361: The server player’s assistance in constructing and deploying the
362: client’s house is part of the broader progression structure.
363: 
364: Do not invent a detailed universal gate-placement formula and label it
365: canon. Gate placement, obstacles, and unlock conditions may be
366: implementation-generated, provided they are consistent and clearly
367: identified as such.
368: 
369: 11. SESSION-WIDE INITIAL CONDITIONS
370: 
371: The session generator should produce a global session record
372: containing: - Session ID and name. - Generation mode. - Seed. - Player
373: roster. - Server/client graph. - Entry order. - Number of players
374: entered. - Prototyping records. - Initial Battlefield state. - Prospit
375: and Derse state. - Initial meteor countdowns, where relevant. - Session
376: difficulty setting. - Complication level. - Generation warnings and
377: notes.
378: 
379: The Battlefield is affected by player entry and prototyping. The
380: generator should therefore use the roster, entry sequence, and
381: prototyping records when establishing the initial Battlefield state.
382: 
383: Do not treat the Battlefield as an unrelated decorative location. It is
384: part of the session’s shared state.
385: 
386: 12. RANDOMIZED AND GUIDED GENERATION MODES
387: 
388: RANDOMIZED SESSION - The creator supplies only required settings, such
389: as player count and session name. - Generate all remaining values using
390: the session seed. - Produce a complete session overview. - Avoid
391: duplicate Classpects by default when possible, without treating
392: duplicates as invalid. - Generate a valid server/client network and
393: entry order. - Ensure each player receives a coherent Land, Consort

396: each player’s details.

messages.summary:
## Objective
- Complete the browser-based human SBURB session generator into a coherent, playable, inspectable session flow.
- Finish wiring the existing generator and verify setup, session interactions, and persistence.

## Requirements
- Support randomized and guided modes, configurable player count, editable seed, and preserve explicit guided choices.
- Generate reproducible, interconnected session data; validate it; support saving/loading and exporting.
- Distinguish canon anchors, interpretations, and implementation rules.
- Provide responsive UI with functional controls and avoid implying unimplemented features are functional.

- Complete the browser-based human SBURB session generator into a coherent, playable, inspectable session flow.

## Process lifecycle

- Run long-lived servers and watchers in a persistent session such as tmux.
- Do not background them in bounded commands without explicit detachment and cleanup.
- After a timeout, inspect the process and endpoint before retrying or claiming failure.

## Linux browser and WebGPU capture

- Use the preinstalled `playwright-cli` executable from Actions or SSH.
- Use its headed Chromium, persistent Xvfb display, and SwiftShader configuration.
- Run `playwright-cli open http://localhost:3002` for the Pascal development server.
- Load a saved scene. Wait for actual geometry and the active WebGPU renderer.
- Run `playwright-cli screenshot --filename=screenshots/linux.png` after creating the output directory.
- Inspect the image. Reject loading screens, empty grids, and blank canvases.
- Report SwiftShader as CPU software rendering. Do not claim GPU hardware acceleration.
- Inspect `$HOME/.local/share/omgithub-playwright/linux.json` for launch settings.
- Use `playwright-cli --help` for commands and named sessions. Pass configuration only to `open`.

## Mobile browser games

- Support Android and iOS phones and tablets with responsive layouts and usable touch controls.
- Keep gameplay and controls visible within safe areas and avoid browser gesture conflicts.
- Add tilt controls only when appropriate; offer touch alternatives and request iOS motion permission from a user gesture when needed.
- Follow explicit device and control requirements in the user request.

SBURB Simulator — Refinement Pass 1

Data Integrity, Generation Rules, and Session Reliability


Development objective: Improve the reliability and internal consistency of the existing human SBURB session generator. This is a refinement of the current application, not a request to rebuild it or introduce the full gameplay system.


Work incrementally. Preserve existing functionality wherever possible, make targeted changes, and test each major change before proceeding.


---


1. Preserve the existing application


Before making changes, inspect the existing project and identify its current architecture, data structures, generation functions, UI components, and persistence mechanisms.


Preserve the following working features:


- Session creation with randomized and guided generation modes.
- Player generation, including names, Classes, Aspects, and dream moons.
- Server/client relationship generation.
- Kernelsprite and prototype generation.
- Land generation, including environments, Consorts, Denizens, NPCs, and Gates.
- Entry sequence tracking.
- Overview, Players, Network, Lands, Entry Sequence, and Reference views.
- Session seed and difficulty information.
- Local session saving and JSON export.


Do not replace functional features with static mockups, sample data, or decorative controls.


Do not discard existing generated content simply because its implementation needs improvement. Preserve useful generation systems and refine them.


If a change requires modifying an existing data structure, update all dependent components consistently. Avoid creating competing versions of the same data.


---


2. Configurable Class and Aspect uniqueness


Add two independent settings to session creation:


- Unique Classes: Enabled by default. When enabled, no two players may share a Class.
- Unique Aspects: Enabled by default. When enabled, no two players may share an Aspect.


When either setting is disabled, duplicates of that category are permitted.


The settings must work independently. For example:


- Unique Classes enabled, Unique Aspects enabled: neither may repeat.
- Unique Classes enabled, Unique Aspects disabled: Classes must be unique, Aspects may repeat.
- Unique Classes disabled, Unique Aspects enabled: Aspects must be unique, Classes may repeat.
- Both disabled: both categories may repeat.


For now, do not generate two players with the exact same Classpect combination, even when both uniqueness settings are disabled.


Generation requirements


- Enforce uniqueness during generation, not merely by filtering duplicates afterward.
- Ensure the generator can produce a valid roster for the selected player count and settings.
- If the selected settings make the requested roster impossible, explain the conflict before generation or offer a valid adjustment.
- Do not silently violate a uniqueness setting to complete generation.
- Store the settings in the session data so they remain available after saving and loading.


User interface


Display both settings clearly in session creation.


Use explanatory descriptions so users understand the difference between Class uniqueness and Aspect uniqueness.


---


3. Improve server/client relationship integrity


The server/client system is an important part of SBURB and should remain a central feature.


Review the existing relationship data and ensure it is represented consistently.


Requirements


- Every player has at most one server.
- The initial host has no server.
- A player cannot serve themselves.
- A player cannot have an invalid or nonexistent server.
- Server dependencies must not create circular chains.
- The server dependency network must be valid and connected to the initial host, unless the system explicitly supports disconnected groups.
- A player cannot enter before their assigned server has entered.


Editing behavior


The current Players view appears to use independent server and client dropdown selectors.


Improve this so that changing a player's server updates the corresponding server's client list automatically, and changing a server's client list updates the affected player's server assignment.


These are two views of the same relationship, not separate independent data.


Prevent contradictory assignments. If a selection would create an invalid relationship, reject it and explain why.


Network view


Ensure the Network view displays the actual underlying relationships, rather than separately generated or hardcoded connections.


A visual network diagram is preferred. It should clearly distinguish:


- Initial host.
- Servers.
- Clients.
- Players waiting for their server to enter.
- Players who have successfully entered.


The network should update when relationships are edited.


---


4. Improve Land generation coherence


This is one of the most important refinements.


The current Land generator produces interesting names, environments, Consorts, Denizens, NPCs, mysteries, and Gates. However, some of these elements do not consistently relate to one another.


A Land should be generated as a coherent place with a central situation, not as a collection of unrelated descriptions.


Required generation order


Generate each Land using a consistent underlying structure:


1. Establish the Land's fundamental identity and environment.
2. Generate its geography, central settlement, and notable landmarks.
3. Establish its central problem or mystery.
4. Determine how that problem affects the inhabitants and environment.
5. Generate Consort society and its relationship to the problem.
6. Generate NPCs with specific roles, personalities, and relevant knowledge.
7. Establish the Denizen, its domain, motivations, and relationship to the Land.
8. Generate the player's main quest and supporting objectives.
9. Generate seven distinct Gate locations and their challenges.
10. Generate enemy themes, resources, and other supporting details.


The order may be implemented differently internally, but the generated results must respect these dependencies.


Coherence requirements


Every generated Land should have:


- A recognizable central problem.
- A plausible connection between the problem and its environment.
- Consorts who have a reason to care about the problem.
- NPCs who know or can discover relevant information.
- A Denizen whose domain, motivations, and challenge relate meaningfully to the Land.
- A main quest that addresses or meaningfully engages with the central problem.
- Gate objectives that contribute to the player's progression.
- Supporting dangers and resources that belong in the Land.


Class and Aspect themes may influence these elements, but must not determine every detail.


For example, a Land belonging to a Prince of Light might involve knowledge, discovery, visibility, or revelation. That does not mean every inhabitant, landmark, enemy, and quest must revolve around Light.


Player-Land ownership


Every Land must be linked to exactly one player using a stable player ID.


All generated Land content must belong to that Land's record.


Do not allow generation rationale, NPCs, quest descriptions, or other content from one player's Land to appear in another player's record.


Review the current display for possible cross-record content mixing. In particular, check whether introductory generation notes or descriptions are accidentally being displayed under the wrong Land.


---


5. Improve Seven Gates


Every Land must have exactly seven distinct Gate progression stages.


Location requirements


- Each Gate must have its own distinct location.
- Each location must be registered as a Land landmark or explicitly generated as a valid additional location.
- Gate locations should make geographical sense.
- Do not repeatedly assign the same location to multiple Gates.
- The Gate locations should be consistent with the Land's geography.


Progression requirements


- Gate 1 is initially accessible.
- Gates 2–7 require completion of the preceding Gate.
- Each Gate must have a distinct objective.
- Objectives should relate to the Land's geography, inhabitants, central problem, or progression.
- Gate 7 should lead toward the player's ultimate progression through the Land and toward Skaia.


Clearly distinguish the following states:


- Locked
- Unlocked
- In progress
- Completed


The interface must not confuse the number of completed Gates with the number of unlocked Gates.


For example, a Land with Gate 1 unlocked and no completed Gates should clearly display that state.


For this refinement pass, Gate objectives may remain descriptive or checklist-based. Do not attempt to implement full exploration gameplay yet.


---


6. Improve Kernelsprite and prototyping records


The current system generates Kernelsprite descriptions and prototype influences, but some records appear to mix completed and planned prototypes.


Separate these concepts.


Each player should have a Kernelsprite record containing:


- Initial Kernelsprite identity or description.
- Prototype slots.
- The object or entity assigned to each prototype slot.
- Prototype status.
- Resulting descriptive traits or influences.


A prototype should have a clear status, such as:


- Available
- Planned
- Completed


Do not apply a prototype's influence to the active Kernelsprite or session until the corresponding prototyping action has actually been completed.


The Overview and Players views should distinguish existing prototype influences from future planned choices.


For this pass, prototype effects can remain descriptive. Actual mechanical consequences will be addressed in a later development milestone.


---


7. Improve NPC generation and writing quality


The existing NPC generation has a useful foundation, but some descriptions contain malformed or awkward sentences.


Avoid constructing prose by concatenating arbitrary sentence fragments.


Instead, store NPC information in structured fields, such as:


- Name
- Species or identity
- Role
- Personality
- Knowledge
- Relationship to the central Land problem
- Relevant quest information


Generate complete, grammatically coherent descriptions from those fields.


NPCs should have meaningful reasons to exist within the Land. Avoid generating several NPCs who perform effectively identical roles without a reason.


NPC names should be unique within their Land unless intentional repetition is supported by the setting.


---


8. Expand session validation


The current validation checks player and Land references, seven Gates, and server-before-client entry order.


Expand it to cover the following:


Player validation


- Every player has a unique stable ID.
- Every player has a valid Class and Aspect.
- Class uniqueness follows the session setting.
- Aspect uniqueness follows the session setting.
- Exact Classpect combinations are not duplicated.
- Every player has a valid dream moon assignment.


Network validation


- Every server reference points to an existing player.
- No player serves themselves.
- No circular dependencies exist.
- Server and client lists agree.
- Every player can trace their dependency chain to the initial host.
- Entry order respects server dependencies.


Land validation


- Every player has exactly one Land.
- Every Land references an existing player.
- Land content is attached to the correct Land ID.
- Every Land has seven Gates.
- Gate locations are distinct and valid.
- Gate progression states are internally consistent.


Prototype validation


- Prototype records have valid statuses.
- Planned prototypes are not treated as completed.
- Applied influences correspond only to completed prototypes.


Reporting


Validation should return a clear report rather than a single generic success or failure message.


For each issue, identify:


- Severity.
- Affected player, Land, or record.
- What is wrong.
- Why it matters.
- Whether it can be corrected automatically.


Use separate categories for errors and warnings.


Do not automatically rewrite generated data without informing the user. Where a correction is safe and unambiguous, offer an explicit repair action.


---


9. Improve saving, exporting, and reproducibility


Preserve local browser saving and JSON export.


Ensure that saving preserves the current session state, not merely the original generated configuration.


The saved session should include:


- Session settings.
- Seed and generation mode.
- Player records.
- Classpect assignments.
- Server/client relationships.
- Kernelsprite and prototype records.
- Land data.
- Gate states.
- Entry progress.
- Any user edits or progression changes.


Distinguish between:


Seeded regeneration: Recreating the original generated session from the same seed and generation settings.


Session restoration: Loading a saved session with all its current modifications and progress intact.


Both should be supported.


If possible, include a schema version in exported JSON so future versions of the application can detect older session formats and migrate them safely.


Do not silently discard fields that are not recognized.


---


10. Update the Mechanics Reference


Preserve the existing distinction between:


- Canon
- Interpretation
- Implementation


Expand the Reference view to accurately describe the application's current features and limitations.


Update it whenever a feature changes.


Do not label an unimplemented mechanic as functional simply because a corresponding button, description, or progress indicator exists.


In particular, clearly distinguish:


- Generated descriptions from simulated mechanics.
- Checklist progression from actual gameplay.
- Estimated countdowns from active in-game time.
- Prototype descriptions from implemented prototype effects.
- Generated Land objectives from interactive exploration.


Continue to distinguish canon facts from interpretations and newly introduced implementation rules.


---


11. Testing and acceptance criteria


Test the changes before considering this refinement pass complete.


At minimum, test the following:


Test A — Default uniqueness


- Generate a six-player session with both uniqueness settings enabled.
- Verify that all Classes are distinct.
- Verify that all Aspects are distinct.
- Verify that no exact Classpect combination repeats.


Test B — Duplicate Classes allowed


- Enable duplicate Classes and disable duplicate Aspects.
- Generate a session.
- Verify that duplicate Classes are permitted while Aspects remain unique.


Test C — Duplicate Aspects allowed


- Enable unique Classes and disable unique Aspects.
- Generate a session.
- Verify that duplicate Aspects are permitted while Classes remain unique.


Test D — Network consistency


- Generate a session with at least six players.
- Verify that server/client relationships agree from both views.
- Change a server assignment and confirm that the network updates correctly.
- Confirm that circular dependencies are rejected.


Test E — Land consistency


- Generate multiple Lands.
- Verify that each Land's central problem, geography, Consorts, NPCs, Denizen, and Gate objectives are coherent.
- Verify that no content is assigned to the wrong player.


Test F — Gate integrity


- Verify that every Land has seven distinct, valid Gate locations.
- Verify that only Gate 1 is initially unlocked.
- Verify that subsequent Gates unlock in order.


Test G — Prototype states


- Verify that planned prototypes do not appear as completed or applied influences.
- Complete a prototype and confirm that its status and displayed influence update.


Test H — Seed reproduction


- Generate a session using a known seed and configuration.
- Record its generated data.
- Generate it again using the same seed and configuration.
- Compare the complete initial generated data, not just player names.
- Verify that the results match.


Test I — Save and restore


- Generate a session.
- Modify relationships and progression states.
- Save and export it.
- Reload the saved session.
- Verify that all modifications and progress remain intact.


---


12. Development discipline


Implement this refinement pass in stages.


Recommended order:


1. Inspect the existing code and data structures.
2. Implement uniqueness settings and generation validation.
3. Correct server/client relationship integrity.
4. Correct Land ownership and coherence.
5. Correct Gate generation and progression states.
6. Separate prototype planning from completion.
7. Improve NPC data and descriptions.
8. Expand validation and reporting.
9. Verify saving, exporting, and reproducibility.
10. Update the Mechanics Reference.


After each stage:


- Test the affected functionality.
- Check that previously working features still function.
- Correct regressions before proceeding.


Do not begin full gameplay implementation during this pass.


Do not redesign the entire interface unless a specific change requires it.


If a requested change cannot be implemented safely without a larger architectural alteration, explain the issue and propose the smallest viable solution instead of silently improvising.


---


Completion report


When finished, provide:


1. A summary of changes implemented.
2. A list of files or components modified.
3. Results of each acceptance test.
4. Any known bugs or incomplete work.
5. Any architectural concerns that should be addressed before the next milestone.


The objective is a reliable, internally consistent session generator that can serve as the foundation for actual SBURB gameplay.

- Gate locations are distinct and valid.
- Gate progression states are internally consistent.


Prototype validation


- Prototype records have valid statuses.
- Planned prototypes are not treated as completed.
- Applied influences correspond only to completed prototypes.


Reporting


Validation should return a clear report rather than a single generic success or failure message.


For each issue, identify:


- Severity.
- Affected player, Land, or record.
- What is wrong.
- Why it matters.
- Whether it can be corrected automatically.


Use separate categories for errors and warnings.


Do not automatically rewrite generated data without informing the user. Where a correction is safe and unambiguous, offer an explicit repair action.


---


9. Improve saving, exporting, and reproducibility


Preserve local browser saving and JSON export.


Ensure that saving preserves the current session state, not merely the original generated configuration.


The saved session should include:


- Session settings.
- Seed and generation mode.
- Player records.
- Classpect assignments.
- Server/client relationships.
- Kernelsprite and prototype records.
- Land data.
- Gate states.
- Entry progress.
- Any user edits or progression changes.


Distinguish between:


Seeded regeneration: Recreating the original generated session from the same seed and generation settings.


Session restoration: Loading a saved session with all its current modifications and progress intact.


Both should be supported.


If possible, include a schema version in exported JSON so future versions of the application can detect older session formats and migrate them safely.


Do not silently discard fields that are not recognized.


---


10. Update the Mechanics Reference


Preserve the existing distinction between:


- Canon
- Interpretation
- Implementation


Expand the Reference view to accurately describe the application's current features and limitations.


Update it whenever a feature changes.


Do not label an unimplemented mechanic as functional simply because a corresponding button, description, or progress indicator exists.


In particular, clearly distinguish:


- Generated descriptions from simulated mechanics.
- Checklist progression from actual gameplay.
- Estimated countdowns from active in-game time.
- Prototype descriptions from implemented prototype effects.
- Generated Land objectives from interactive exploration.


Continue to distinguish canon facts from interpretations and newly introduced implementation rules.


---


11. Testing and acceptance criteria


Test the changes before considering this refinement pass complete.


At minimum, test the following:


Test A — Default uniqueness


- Generate a six-player session with both uniqueness settings enabled.
- Verify that all Classes are distinct.
- Verify that all Aspects are distinct.
- Verify that no exact Classpect combination repeats.


Test B — Duplicate Classes allowed


- Enable duplicate Classes and disable duplicate Aspects.
- Generate a session.
- Verify that duplicate Classes are permitted while Aspects remain unique.


Test C — Duplicate Aspects allowed


- Enable unique Classes and disable unique Aspects.
- Generate a session.
- Verify that duplicate Aspects are permitted while Classes remain unique.


Test D — Network consistency


- Generate a session with at least six players.
- Verify that server/client relationships agree from both views.
- Change a server assignment and confirm that the network updates correctly.
- Confirm that circular dependencies are rejected.


Test E — Land consistency


- Generate multiple Lands.
- Verify that each Land's central problem, geography, Consorts, NPCs, Denizen, and Gate objectives are coherent.
- Verify that no content is assigned to the wrong player.


Test F — Gate integrity


- Verify that every Land has seven distinct, valid Gate locations.
- Verify that only Gate 1 is initially unlocked.
- Verify that subsequent Gates unlock in order.


Test G — Prototype states


- Verify that planned prototypes do not appear as completed or applied influences.
- Complete a prototype and confirm that its status and displayed influence update.


Test H — Seed reproduction


- Generate a session using a known seed and configuration.
- Record its generated data.
- Generate it again using the same seed and configuration.
- Compare the complete initial generated data, not just player names.
- Verify that the results match.


Test I — Save and restore


- Generate a session.
- Modify relationships and progression states.
- Save and export it.
- Reload the saved session.
- Verify that all modifications and progress remain intact.


---


12. Development discipline


Implement this refinement pass in stages.


Recommended order:


1. Inspect the existing code and data structures.
2. Implement uniqueness settings and generation validation.
3. Correct server/client relationship integrity.
4. Correct Land ownership and coherence.
5. Correct Gate generation and progression states.
6. Separate prototype planning from completion.
7. Improve NPC data and descriptions.
8. Expand validation and reporting.
9. Verify saving, exporting, and reproducibility.
10. Update the Mechanics Reference.


After each stage:


- Test the affected functionality.
- Check that previously working features still function.
- Correct regressions before proceeding.


Do not begin full gameplay implementation during this pass.


Do not redesign the entire interface unless a specific change requires it.


If a requested change cannot be implemented safely without a larger architectural alteration, explain the issue and propose the smallest viable solution instead of silently improvising.


---


Completion report


When finished, provide:


1. A summary of changes implemented.
2. A list of files or components modified.
3. Results of each acceptance test.
4. Any known bugs or incomplete work.
5. Any architectural concerns that should be addressed before the next milestone.

## Objective
- Refine the existing browser-based human SBURB session generator for data integrity, coherent generation, reliable progression, and transparent validation without rebuilding it or adding full gameplay.

## Requirements
- Preserve existing generation modes, player/session content, views, progression, local saves, and JSON export.
- Add independent, default-enabled Unique Classes and Unique Aspects settings; always prevent duplicate exact Classpect combinations.
- Enforce one connected, acyclic server network with one initial host and consistent server/client records.
- Improve Land ownership and coherence, seven distinct Gate locations and sequential states, prototype statuses, NPC quality, validation reports, persistence, reproducibility, and Mechanics Reference accuracy.
- Test acceptance scenarios A–I and report changes, test results, incomplete work, and architectural concerns.

## Decisions
- Preserve the modular plain HTML/CSS/JavaScript application and make targeted changes.
- Guided fixed choices that conflict with uniqueness or network integrity should produce clear errors rather than silently being changed.

## Work State
### Completed
- Added default-checked Unique Classes and Unique Aspects controls in `index.html`.
- Added `validationReport(s)` and `validateSession(s)` in `app.js`.
- Renamed the legacy generator to `generateLegacy(config)` and added `buildGeneratedSession(...)` for generated Lands, sprites, Gates, entry state, session settings, and metadata.
- Generated sessions include `schemaVersion: 2`; generated Gate locations are distinct and NPC names are tracked for uniqueness.
- Confirmed `node --check app.js` passes after the latest edits.

### Active
- Fix `readSetup()` and saved settings to use `uniqueClasses` and `uniqueAspects`; remove stale `uniqueTitles` references.
- Review generator and validation behavior, including sprite prototype/influence consistency, network integrity, and validation UI/report.
- Refine Mechanics Reference and persistence/import compatibility.
- Run browser and acceptance tests A–I.

### Blocked
- Generation/build and runtime behavior remain unverified; syntax success does not confirm the latest implementation works.

## Next Move
1. Update `readSetup()` to read the new checkboxes; verify settings survive save/export/import.
2. Exercise seeded random and guided generation; test network, Lands/Gates, sprite prototypes, progression, and report UI.
3. Complete UI/reference refinements and acceptance tests A–I; report results and architectural concerns.

## Relevant Files
- `app.js`: Generator, validation, UI, progression, and persistence.
- `index.html`: Setup controls and session UI structure.
- `style.css`: Existing styles; may need updates for validation/settings presentation.

## Important Context
- Changes are uncommitted; repository files are untracked.
- `app.js` contains duplicate `init()` declarations.
- `readSetup()` still reads `#uniqueTitles`, while `index.html` defines `#uniqueClasses` and `#uniqueAspects`.
- The active generator returns `buildGeneratedSession(...)` and calls `validateSession(session)`; only syntax has been checked.

2: 
3: - Run long-lived servers and watchers in a persistent session such as tmux.
4: - Do not background them in bounded commands without explicit detachment and cleanup.
5: - After a timeout, inspect the process and endpoint before retrying or claiming failure.

7: ## Linux browser and WebGPU capture
8: 
9: - Use the preinstalled `playwright-cli` executable from Actions or SSH.
10: - Use its headed Chromium, persistent Xvfb display, and SwiftShader configuration.
11: - Run `playwright-cli open http://localhost:3002` for the Pascal development server.
12: - Load a saved scene. Wait for actual geometry and the active WebGPU renderer.
13: - Run `playwright-cli screenshot --filename=screenshots/linux.png` after creating the output directory.
14: - Inspect the image. Reject loading screens, empty grids, and blank canvases.
15: - Report SwiftShader as CPU software rendering. Do not claim GPU hardware acceleration.
16: - Inspect `$HOME/.local/share/omgithub-playwright/linux.json` for launch settings.
17: - Use `playwright-cli --help` for commands and named sessions. Pass configuration only to `open`.
18: 
19: ## Mobile browser games
20: 
21: - Support Android and iOS phones and tablets with responsive layouts and usable touch controls.
22: - Keep gameplay and controls visible within safe areas and avoid browser gesture conflicts.
23: - Add tilt controls only when appropriate; offer touch alternatives and request iOS motion permission from a user gesture when needed.

10: - Use its headed Chromium, persistent Xvfb display, and SwiftShader configuration.
11: - Run `playwright-cli open http://localhost:3002` for the Pascal development server.
12: - Load a saved scene. Wait for actual geometry and the active WebGPU renderer.
13: - Run `playwright-cli screenshot --filename=screenshots/linux.png` after creating the output directory.
14: - Inspect the image. Reject loading screens, empty grids, and blank canvases.
15: - Report SwiftShader as CPU software rendering. Do not claim GPU hardware acceleration.
16: - Inspect `$HOME/.local/share/omgithub-playwright/linux.json` for launch settings.
17: - Use `playwright-cli --help` for commands and named sessions. Pass configuration only to `open`.

22: - Keep gameplay and controls visible within safe areas and avoid browser gesture conflicts.
